search.text: AKAN (cluster of people): FANTE; ASANTE; BAULE, an Akan-related group, are embedded in the forest zone and linked politically and culturally to Akan polities to the east. NZEMA (APPOLO) Côte d’Ivoire; Ghana; EDO Together with other ancient empires (Ancient Ghana, Mali, Songhai, Ashanti), Great Benin of Edo people flourished in the part of the present-day Nigeria from 1200s to 1800s, and participated in long-distance trade of gold, ivory and salt, accumulating wealth through this trade. Musicians of Benin Kingdom have a presence as cultural representations through the museum display of bronze plaques showing horn players and drummers. Nigeria EWE The GBE groups, including FON, GUN, and the EWE of Togo and modern Ghana, trace their common origin to Tado in modern Togo, on the left bank of the river Mono. In the 1500s, disputes within Tado lead to migrations: one section moves west to found Notsie, which becomes the center for Ewe dispersal over the region between the Mono and Volta rivers in Togo and Ghana. The Ewe who move west from this Togo-based center live precariously as a minority within powerful kingdoms of neighboring peoples and evolve more than 120 microstates differing in dialect and cultural traits, while related kin to the east create larger, more centralized units. Ewe exodus in the late 1600s from the tyrannical king Agokoli of Nots, using fierce drumming to intimidate his warriors during escape. Migrating southwest, Ewe groups found settlements along a large lagoon near the mouth of the Volta River; the group led by Wenya, too tired to go farther, becomes known as the ANLO (cramped). Other Ewe families settle along the Atlantic coast and upland hills of this region, laying the basis for later communities in what became Ghana and Togo. Hunters, regarded as repositories of knowledge given by God, possessing special herbs and the ability to communicate safely with dangerous animals, conduct traditional customs involving drumming, double bell, and worship, and in legends they are the ones who first bring the forest/monkey dance and drumming that becomes Agbekor (traditional war dance/drumming) back to the community. The 18th and 19th centuries see frequent military conflicts with neighboring groups, with European traders, and among Ewe themselves; the Anlo-Ewe gain a fearsome reputation as warriors, forming the backdrop for war drumming traditions. Britain, Germany, and France administer Ewe territory during a brief colonial period from the 1880s to the 1950s, after which Ewe people live in the independent nation-states of Ghana and Togo. Christian missionaries whip students for attending traditional performance events, discouraging participation in Ewe music and dance. After Ghanas statehood in 1957, national government sponsors professional troupes in which Agbekor is a staple, contributing to broader Ewe cultural visibility. Contemporary Ewe traditional music idioms with freshly composed songs, contrasted explicitly with Agbekor as an old repertory inherited from ancestors. Much of Ewe life focuses on dance clubs that function as entertainment, recreation, and ceremonial institutions; Each Ewe dance club has composers who create music in three named genres: axatsevu, akpewu, and specific style pieces characterized by distinctive drumming and dancing. Funeral music in Anlo communities – dance-club repertories (e.g., Adzomani) performed at funerals; “good music” at funerals is described as the deepest expression of loss, and a funeral without music is lamented as “(what) a sad thing.” Vodun religion (AJA, EWE, FON): voodoo rhythms, Zangbeto (guardian of the nights). Benin; Ghana; Nigeria; Togo IGBO In Igbo and other Eastern Forest societies, music is used widely—at royal honors, assemblies, funerals, festivals and storytelling—and often involves masked performance and satirical topical songs; In Igbo society, music making is not a class or profession: individuals specialize according to talent and act as interpreters of the community’s music; training is informal, mainly by imitation, reflecting decentralized, non-urban political organization. Musical traits show influences from Central Africa: equal prominence of membranophones (igba) and slit-drums (ekwe, ufie), rich percussive instruments (drums, bells, rattles, percussion vessels, wooden clappers), and melodic instruments (xylophones, lamellophones, flutes, trumpets, musical bows, pluriarcs). Cameroon; Gabon; Equatorial Guinea; Nigeria YORUBA people described as (predominantly) in SW Nigeria and partly in Kwara/Kogi (Nigeria), representing the Yoruba-Edo-Nupe subcluster. Ile-Ife is the religious center, and people believe in common descent from Oduduwa. The political system is based on kingdoms ruled by divine kings, with the Ogboni secret society, a military organization and age-grades supporting royal power. The YORUBA kingdom of Oyo, a major coastal state, rises before 1500 and declines in the early 1800s after civil wars; it maintains trade with Songhai, Hausa, and Nupe, linking Yoruba communities into wider northsouth networks. In Benin they maintain indigenous culture, especially religion, more fully than in Nigeria. Among the Yoruba (living mostly in southwest Nigeria), Islam has made inroads, but Christian missionary activity since the 1840s has checked its further advance, marking an important 19th-century religious shift. Fulani conquest (1804–1808) under Usman Dan Fodio, incorporating the region into the Sokoto Caliphate. Dan Fodio’s campaign “profoundly shaped” Yoruba political geography. Yoruba adopt waka from the Hausa “probably in the early 1800s.” Genres and styles found among Yoruba include texts dominating praise chants, acclamations, and songs while instruments primarily accompany the voice. “Drummunication” among South Western Yoruba people (Nigeria) described as an extra-mundane tool linking people with deities/spirits/ancestors, as communication between natural/supernatural worlds; extra-mundane channels include incantation, spiritual chants, prayers, invocations, séances, trances, panegyric praise, dirges sacrifices. Among musicians, most are semiprofessional, relying on farming or weaving. Recruitment, especially of drummers, is patrilineal, and training is formal, usually through kin or established musicians. Most specialize either in particular instruments or in specific kinds of vocal music. Yoruba priests and religious specialists play central roles in music for orisa worship and oro ceremonies (Songs for oro, the secret society of night hunters that administers justice in Oron Nation), linking musical authority closely to ritual authority and associated with bullroarers and mirlitons. Repertoires for Orisa worship, including possession and dance with chanted text. Yoruba voices often harmonize in fourths (rather than the thirds favored by some neighboring groups), giving vocal lines greater mobility. there is a contrast between unison singing in the east and polyphony in the west, where harmonies in fourths allow greater mobility. Benin; Nigeria

search.title: INLANDS AND DESERT
search.text: FULƁE (FULA/FULANI/PEUL), who are in the minority throughout the savanna from Senegal to Cameroon, originating in the middle Senegal area and formed through Tukulor–Berber intermixture, spread eastward and southward between the 1100s and the 1800s, settling among Soninke, Mandinka, Bambara, Hausa, and Mossi. From the 1100s, Fulani spread across the savanna and later wage jihads to gain political dominance, reshaping Central Sudanic musical-political culture. Futa Jallon jihad (Guinea, 1725) launches the first West African jihad. Early in the 1800s, the Fulani conquered the Hausa and organized their territory into emirates. Among muslim FULANI, professional drummers specialize in childrens dance songs and in castigation contests (soro/sharo), where they sing praises of young men and build morale and tension. For Fulani court musicians, songs praising chiefs and wealthy patrons, referring to genealogies and heroic exploits, form a central genre; some are attached to single patrons while others travel between courts. secular adaptations of previously religious poems also appear. Around 1800, the genre of Fulfulde sung poems GIME arises and becomes part of the Central Sudanic Islamic literary-musical tradition. sung on religious themes and secular topics, in private or small gatherings and on special religious occasions, becomes a specialty of blind beggars as well as other performers. early examples come from Futa Djallon and Sokoto, but they represent a broader Fulani tradition within the Central Sudanic area. Fulani herdsmen also perform a range of song types—work songs, lullabies, love songs, cattle-praise songs, children’s dance songs and dance songs (ruume, yake, geerewol) for youth. Benin; Burkina Faso; Guinea Bissau; Guinea Conakry; Mali; Niger; Nigeria HAUSA: founded major city-states including Kano (AD 993), Zaria (AD 1000), Katsina (AD 1100). The Hausa (a Central Sudanic people for whom Hausa is the mother tongue) at one point lived within the Songhai Empire, while also paying tribute to the king of Bornu. Bori, identified later as a pre-Islamic religion among the Hausa that makes much use of music and dance, has roots in this pre- and early-Islamic era, even though it continues beyond it. In the pre-emirate Hausa area, the spread of Islam (from Mali in the 1300s and via Kanuri) creates a contrast between Islamic ritual—where music is largely absent except for the call to prayer—and older practices such as bori, a pre-Islamic spirit-possession religion that makes much use of music and dance. Islamization of the Hausa area begins well before 1800: many scholars believe Islam entered from Mali in the 1300s, possibly earlier via the Kanuri of the Bornu Empire; for a time the Hausa lived under Songhai rule and also paid tribute to the king of Bornu. Hausa music includes forms later labelled state ceremonial music (rokon fada), court praise (yabon sarakai), and rural folk/popular music; these genres emerge in continuity with earlier political contexts under Songhai and Bornu influence and are framed by courtly structures that predate the Fulɓe conquest. In the early 1800s, the Fulani (Sokoto Caliphate) conquest of the Hausa reorganized their territory into emirates; Hausa associated with Fulani “after the Fulani Jihad of the early 1800s”; Nineteenth-century Hausa practice within the emirate system gives rise to state ceremonial music (rokon fada), court praise (yabon sarakai) and rural folk/popular music. In Hausa practice, apart from bori, music and dance have no direct association with religion; music other than the call to prayer is rarely heard in mosques or during Islamic ritual, even though Islamic holidays and political and religious life frame much musical activity. Bori remains an enduring genre: a pre-Islamic spirit-possession religion whose ceremonies use specific music to communicate with spirits; musicians for bori form a distinct professional category in Hausa culture. In Hausa practice (aside from bori), music and dance have no direct association with religion; music (other than the call to prayer) is rarely heard in mosques or during Islamic ritual, even though Islamic holidays and political/religious life frame much musical activity. Bori, a pre-Islamic spirit-possession religion, makes much use of music and dance and is an enduring religious genre within the Central Sudanic zone. Scholars distinguish several types of Hausa professional musicians: (1) musicians of occupational classes, (2) musicians in political life, (3) musicians of recreational music, (4) musician-entertainers, and (5) musicians for bori spirit possession. Two types of praise songs are distinguished in the emirate context: urban classical praise (performed by professionals attached to a single patron, with relatively fixed stylistic and textual traits) and popular praise songs (performed by freelance musicians with many patrons, of more recent origin). Popular music rivals court praise in audience and artistry; instruments such as kalangu, goge, kukuma and kuntigi distinguish popular ensembles from court ensembles. Traditional Hausa music such as Kalangu, Shantu and Mandiri” described as existing “before the transformation of the media industry and the technology.” Praise singing described as embedded in Hausa music for political elites (palace-linked comparison). ****Specialists in acclaiming patrons are maroki (pl. maroka); professional male singer-composers are mawaki (pl. mawaka); instrumentalists on drums, lutes, and idiophones are makadi (pl. makada); aerophone players are mai busa (pl. masu busa); female specialists include magu da (ululators), zabiya (professional female singers), and marokya (female acclaimer). Burkina Faso; Niger; Nigeria KANURI (??CENTRAL AFRICA??) described as descendants of the Kanem Bornu empire (AD 800–1800). Cameroon; Chad; Niger; Nigeria SONGHAI began to dominate large parts of Sudanic Africa during the 1200s, reached its apogee in the early 1500s, extending from near the Atlantic in the west to include most Hausa states in the east and felt North African influence. its political and musical influence underpins later Hausa/Fulani. In the 1400s and 1500s, as Mossi kingdoms rose to power, Mossi armies repeatedly fought the Songhai for control of the Niger Bend, connecting Voltaic Mossi polities with Songhai power centred along the Niger Songhai music is divided into secular and religious (follay) categories. Secular music includes solo, choral (may be unaccompanied or accompanied by the KONTIGI lute) and instrumental pieces for wrestling matches and dances, work songs by men and women, and songs by children and adolescents in games and courtship; texts treat history, politics, legends, fables, satire and praise. Follay is religious music performed for a hierarchy of divinities associated with natural forces (sky, rain, thunder, earth, river, rainbow). Each spirit is called by specific melodies and rhythms; this tradition shows links to Hausa bori spirit-possession practices. Benin; Burkina Faso; Mali; Niger; Nigeria TOUAREG (Kel TamasheQ) described as migrating south (8th–12th c AD) from Magrehb and carrying Amazigh (BERBER) culture. Profound attachment to music and poetry linked to Amazigh roots; emphasis on poetry as cultural anchor. Described as nomadic, traveling throughout the Sahel; Touareg tradition of “vivid and refined courtly love poetry” praising women’s qualities (in Tamashek language). music playable by anyone (no professional caste). Belluwel and akhaguwwen singing techniques documented in 70s recorded releases. Algerie; Burkina Faso; Libya; Mali; Niger

search.title: MANDE
search.text: MANDE region is the centre of several great empires: 300s to 1200s - kingdom of Ghana; 1000s - Mandinka had organized a small state called Mali; around 1235 - Mali Empire was founded by Sunjata Keita, unifying warring communities and arosing in the West African savanna between desert and forest, a cultural crossroads where Sudanic African, Tuareg, Berber, Arab and European civilizations met, connected by caravan routes between the Mediterranean and the Sudan and by rivers such as the Niger, Senegal and Gambia. Within this imperial setting, JALIYAA (the professional art of jalolu) already played important roles in Mande civilization, serving the needs of elite patrons. Sunjata Keita and his personal jeli Bala Faseke Kouyaté (balafon player, captured by Sunjata enemy Susu Sumanguru because of his high value) anchor the origin myth of jeli lineages (all Kouyaté jelis are said to descend from Bala Faseke). Dyeli/jali form a hereditary caste of musicians, praise-singers, historians, royal counselors, educators, public entertainers and instrument-makers attached to aristocrats, warriors, and patrons, specializing in praise and historical songs with instruments like KORA and BALAFON. Long epic narratives, genealogies and praise songs about rulers such as Sunjata Keita and his generals form the core repertoire. Kings maintain courts where jelis entertain and educate nobility. Jaliyaa music is framed as one of the world’s “classical” musics, defined partly by performance for elites and by a sophisticated, orally transmitted theoretical system, despite the absence of written notation or formal treatises. 1353 - Ibn Battuta visits Mali and describes Muslim feast days, Mansa Sulayman as “sultan”, Dugha as intermediary and master of royal musicians with lutes, drums, trumpets and bugles; this early Islamic context forms part of the historical heritage shared by Mande peoples. Mali is described as fabulously wealthy and as a centralized, hierarchically organized empire with distinct social classes, Islamic libraries and universities in great cosmopolitan cities, and a class of literati (writing in Arabic) who managed commerce and law. Dyula people of Burkina Faso have their capital at Bobo-Dioulasso, a strategic commercial and cultural center whose strongest traditions are those of balafon and percussion. Mande society is stratified: basic distinction between foro/foro (freeborn) and jongo (slaves); the ruler (mansa/sultan) and warriors are at the top of society and have music performed specifically for them; nobles (horon), artisan “castes” (nyamakala) including jelis, and descendants of slaves (jon). Hunter societies (donsoton) function as inter-ethnic, egalitarian associations (excluding only women and children) whose members serve as guardians of villages, providers of meat and healers; their blues-like melodies and powerful rhythmic music is seen as among Africa’s oldest surviving musical forms and probably the ancestor of jeli music. Dance drumming and singing are identified as the non-classical counterpart to Jaliyaa: male drum troupes perform for village events, especially for women’s dancing, with women as the main subjects and participants of songs. 1400s - The Mali Empire went into decline, marking the end of Mali’s regional imperial dominance and followed by SONGHAI rule (1460–1591). Mande diaspora begins, with lesser kingdoms remaining and trade networks kept intact. Jaliyaa follows regional power holders (war chiefs, merchants, later politicians) across the Mande world, spreading its culture, together with Islam, across West Africa. 1700s - French writings coin ‘griot’ as the term for hereditary professional musicians. Possible Arabic root of the term: some scholars suggest ‘griot’ may derive from Arabic ‘qawal’ (“word, speak, sound”), linking Dyula-related terminology partly to Arab linguistic influence. European travellers of the 18th–19th centuries see leaders with jali at their side, or jalolu improvising praise songs for nobles in streets; this practice is labelled “begging” in English but is in fact a cultural obligation of jaliyaa. During the colonial period, traditional social structure broke down; both the role of the professional musician and the patronage system changed. Musicians no longer depended on the patronage of specific individuals, had to hunt for patrons, and begging became more common. This social structure and the patron–jeli relationship survive into the 21st century, with presidents among those receiving countless praise songs. Standard jeli pieces – Songs like “Lamban”, “Sunjata”, “Turamaghan” and “Bambougoudji” are centuries-old but treated as improvisatory “blueprints”, constantly updated like jazz standards at weddings. Core jali families (Kouyaté, Suso/Sissoko, Jebateh/Jobarteh/Diabaté) dominate musical professions across the Mande world. Les Ballets Africains structures Mande drumming and dancing into a theatrical ballet-style show for international audiences, a staging model that spreads to national troupes in all Mande-inhabited countries. JAZZ genealogies projected onto jaliaa: foreign scholars and listeners sometimes interpret Mande styles as ancestral to jazz. In recent years, Islamic extremist groups have terrorised musicians in Mali, compared explicitly to the Taliban’s suppression of music in Afghanistan. ****************The type of instrument used in performance determines the musical scale; for example, Maninka of Guinea tune xylophones to an equitonal heptatonic scale and the kora to a nonequitonal heptatonic scale, suggesting sophisticated heptatonic systems in the Manding instrumental tradition. Bamana jeli music, anchored in central Mali with slow pentatonic melodies, strong dance rhythms and NGONI accompaniment. SONINKE, older, founders of Ghana Empire (300 to 1240), bring Islam in the area around 1000 Gambia; Mali; Mauritania; Senegal MANINKA (Malinke) Mali's empire founders, centered around Guinea and Mali. BAMBARA (Bamana) emerged as a distinct political and cultural entity following the collapse of the Mali Empire, peaking during Segou Empire (1700s). Mali official language. MANDINKA appeared as a distinct group when the Mali Empire expanded westward toward the Atlantic coast (Senegambia-Guinea Bissau). They established the Kaabu Kingdom, which remained a major power until the mid-19th century. Côte d’Ivoire; Gambia; Guinea Bissau; Guinea Conakry; Mali; Senegal DYULA, (meaning "merchant" in Bambara) class of muslim merchants emerged during 1300s, mix of the precedent people. Burkina Faso; Côte d’Ivoire; Mali KPELLE migrations into the area known as Liberia occurred between the 1400s and the 1800s, bringing Kpelle musical and social institutions into Liberian territory. Poro and Sande secret societies are established as vehicles for transmitting culture. Woi-meni-pele epic genre. Kpelle timekeepers concepts of time (months named after sound qualities; “year” as a “fence” enclosing social action) are linked to how performances are structured. proverb “if you build a town and there’s no drummer in it, then it’s not a town”. Guinea Conakry; Liberia DAN (linking Ivorian forest society to wider Mande networks), who straddle the borders of Côte d’Ivoire and Liberia, distinguish three main types of music: tan (‘dance song’, also ‘instrumental music’ and ‘dance’), zlee (‘praise song’), and gbo (‘funeral lament’). Music-making is a highly regarded profession. Ge (mask institutions) are central religious and political authorities; chiefs’ power is legitimated through association with powerful village ge, with masks appearing at harvest celebrations and life-cycle rites like weddings and funerals. French colonial administrators mount large mask festivals. Côte d’Ivoire; Liberia SUSU, Guinea Conakry; Sierra Leone MENDE, (Poro) Sierra Leone VAI, (Poro) invented their own writing system in 1800s Liberia; Sierra Leone

search.title: VOLTAIC CLUSTER
search.text: Western Sudanic (Manding) and Central Sudanic musical styles continue to influence Voltaic areas through Manding speakers and Fulani/Hausa/Songhai minorities. The Voltaic cluster is described as dispersed across Burkina Faso, Mali, and the northern regions of Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Togo, and Benin (under the Gur languages umbrella).Voltaic high-tessitura, mostly pentatonic styles (partly in Mali). The MOSSI / BARIBA are distinguished by their location in the Benin Gap, an area covering roughly present-day Benin, Togo, and southeast Ghana, where the savanna breaks through the forest to the Atlantic; rivers and lagoons there foster intense movement and cultural interchange between forest and savanna populations.Mossi kingdoms rise to power in the 1400s–1500s and fight the Songhai over control of the Niger Bend, while pushing southward against Gourmantché and Kusasi—peoples within the Voltaic cluster dispersed in Burkina. • LoDagaa-related societies (including Lobi, Gan, Gouin, Wara etc.) occupy northwest Ghana and adjacent parts of Burkina Faso, already sharing Voltaic cultural traits and funeral xylophone traditions that tie these frontier zones into a common cultural area. Bariba occupy Borgu (northwest of Yorubaland) in the 1500s; their kingdom later reaches its height in the 1700s. Growing acceptance of Islam in Mossi kingdoms opens communication between MossiBariba Voltaic groups and Western/Central Sudanic clusters, affecting Bariba communities. Larle Naaba, traditional head of all Mossi griot musicians, maintains his function vis-à-vis Mossi kings as genealogist, counsellor, historian and musician; he leads his own troupe and teaches musicians in his own royal court, exemplifying hereditary court musician roles. Professional musicians form a distinct social class and dominate musical life. They attach themselves to royalty or important persons, enjoy high social status and function as historians, genealogists, and moral commentators through their praise songs. Vocal and instrumental music is characterized by high tessitura, predominantly pentatonic scale systems, tense vocal quality, and modest ornamentation. Islamic celebrations frequently integrate traditional music, especially historical or genealogy songs performed by drummers and fiddlers at Islamic events, underlining a syncretic religious-musical style. Benin; Burkina Faso; Côte d’Ivoire; Mali; Nigeria; Togo SENUFO communities maintain Poro and Sande (brang by MANE, mande XVIc invaders) initiation-society music: water-drum and xylophone-based ensembles at “coming-out” and funerals, with pentatonic scales, instrumental polyphony (especially xylophones), and monodic vocal music. Among Senufo communities, there is a caste system for some occupations but no separate musician caste; instead, music is integrated into Poro and other social structures, with specialists embedded in ritual roles rather than a separate hereditary musician class. Burkina Faso; Côte d’Ivoire; Mali DOGON communities maintain strong continuity of identity, customs, and religion, with limited outside influence on their musical culture. emphasize bullroarer and drum-centered music, masked dances, and collective dancing. Burkina Faso; Mali In KASENA music, royal and state occasions (durbars, festivals, events honoring dignitaries) become important musical contexts cultivated during colonial rule, indicating how praise songs and ensemble pieces come to represent traditional authority and develop within new colonial structures. Musicians are semiprofessional, they farm or work in other jobs and play when needed. They hold high social status as respected community members rather than as a marginalized caste. Royal/state music among Kasena becomes more prominent in colonial rule, with aerophone–drum ensembles playing heptatonic, polyphonic music (third-based harmony resolving to unison). Benin(?), Burkina Faso; Ghana DAGBAMBA do not have a single word equivalent to the Western idea of “music,” since music, dance and drama are closely bound. Dagbon emerges as a hierarchical, centralized kingdom of the Dagbamba in northern Ghana; lunsi drummers are integral to this state structure. Lunsi (griots) in Dagbaŋ are identified as custodians of culture who transmit histories from generation to generation, occupying a central socio-musical role within Northern Ghanaian society. Royal musicians attached to ancient kingdoms and to Dagbaŋ royal courts enhance state occasions and provide musical commentary on event Through south-Saharan trade routes and ethnic migrations, and via Wangara and Hausa clerics, Islamic influences reach the north of contemporary Ghana; Naa Zanjina (1648–1677) adopts Islam as state religion in Dagbaŋ. Ghana; Togo In DAGAABA subcluster areas, long histories of migration and warfare make clans vulnerable to slave raiding until British colonial government in Ghana implants chieftainships. Historically, the origins of Dagaaba people has been a complex mystery to tackle, probably related to a schism with Dagbamba. In LoDagaa areas, the local rise of Islam in the late twentieth century alters religious and musical life, contributing to a decline in xylophone-based practices associated with animism. Burkina Faso; Côte d’Ivoire; Ghana

search.title: WEST ATLANTIC
search.text: much Wolof/Fula/Tukulor(Haalpulaar) music described as “derived from Mande music.” Before about 1400, groups in this area, particularly those in Liberia, Sierra Leone and west Côte d’Ivoire, felt little influence from the savanna empires of Ghana and Mali; this isolation allowed the development of small, widely scattered states. With the disintegration of the Mali Empire in the 1400s, Malinke traders and warriors moved from the savanna into the kola plantations of the forest, bringing merchandise and Islam, affecting areas in and around Liberia. WOLOF are described as a fusion of Serer, Mande and Fulɓe elements. Their ancestors occupied the southern area of present-day Mauritania, cohabiting with Fulɓe; in the 1300s they developed their Jolof states, and by about 1450 their kingdom’s fiefs stretched from the Senegal River to the Gambia River. Gambia; Mauritania; Senegal TEMNE migrated from the Futa Jallon region of Guinea, who left their original settlements to escape FULƁE invasions in the 15th century, and migrated south before settling between the Kolenté and Rokel River area of Sierra Leone. Their music, representing one of the largest groups in Sierra Leone, shows a dual character. On one hand it shares Western Forest cluster traits such as prominent percussion, masked dancers and secret-society music. On the other hand it incorporates features associated with the Western Sudanic cluster: occasional use of the fiddle (named angbulu, gbulu, rafon in Temne) and a tendency of women to imitate a Sudanic singing style. These Western Sudanic traits are said to have been adopted through interaction with Fulɓe during Temne territorial expansion east and northeast, and through Fulɓe dispersal in Sierra Leone. Sierra Leone GOLA (Poro) Liberia; Sierra Leone BALANTA, Guinea Bissau

search.title: Benin
search.text: Benin’s position astride savanna (north) and forest (south) means that its musical life continually reflects both savanna political traditions (empires, Islamic courts, professional praise specialists) and forest traditions (fragmented polities, masquerades, secret societies, and complex rhythmic ensembles). In the “Benin Gap” (covering roughly present-day Benin, Togo, and SE Ghana), the savanna cuts through the forest to the Atlantic, and rivers and lagoons facilitate movement and cultural interchange between forest and savanna societies. Studies on societies in southern Benin (as part of the Eastern Forest cluster) show that this region exemplifies forest-belt patterns: complex percussion-based ensembles, elaborate court music and masquerades, and secret societies and age-grades as key institutions, with some adoption of Islam and Christianity.- 1600-1904: Dahomey Kingdom (FON People). - 1960-1972- first years of independent Dahomey, with a quite vibrant music scene. Urban nightlife thrives through dance-band styles strongly influenced by Ghanaian and Nigerian HIGHLIFE, AFRO-CUBAN music, CONGOLESE-RUMBA, American SOUL and French CHANSON. An Afro-Cuban direction is paved by El Rego et ses Commandos and further developed by Gnonnas Pedro y sus Panchos. City bands such as Picoby Band d'Abomey, Super Star de Ouidah and Anassua Jazz de Parakou embody these Afro-Cuban / highlife-inflected nightclub styles. Benin is described as having a strong base in Vodoun / Voodoo rhythms, which are used and re-interpreted by groups and artists both inside Benin and in the diaspora across the eras, including Le Roi Alokpon, Amikpon and Gbétchéou. HONGAN and KAKAGBO percussion ritually used by the GUN “Zangbeto”, Vodoun guardians of the night, later reworked into modern patterns by Sagbohan Danialou. - 1972–1990- Kérékou’s dictatorship, explicitly described as a “Marxist-Leninist” regime, renaming Dahomey as Benin. Artists are expected to praise those in power; a strict curfew leads to the end of “wild nightlife” and the scene at home “grinds to a halt.” Many musicians move abroad (e.g., settling in Paris and elsewhere), partly as a response to political pressure. Under the regime, a push toward “seeking their own traditions” leads to hybrid tradi-modern styles (as documented on the Sonorama Sud Bénin CD/DVD): TCHINKOUME, rooted in funeral contexts, becomes a creative source for new electric/percussion-heavy dance music like TCHINK-SYSTEM, created by Tohon Stan. ZINLI (Traditional royal court music), originally restricted to royal funerals at the Abomey king’s court, later becomes the basis for modern works by artists like Alèkpéhanhou. Urban Groove of T.P. Orchestre Poly-Rythmo mixes Afro-soul, AFRO-BEAT, SOUKOUS, Cuban sounds and FUNK. Nel Oliver absorbs a range of Afro-American influences to create this powerful hybrid AFRO-AKPALA-FUNK style. Mainstream 1970s African pop Cella Stella, stylistically aligned with the broader African pop of that era. -1990s/early 2000s- About fifteen years of democracy, even if Kéréku is legally elected again in 1996, are credited with strengthening an enthusiastic new tradi-modern sound. Modernized fishermen’s AGBADJA from the southwest becomes very popular through artists like Gbessi-Zolawadji. Gangbe Brass Band mixes big-band JAZZ sounds with traditional percussion patterns, Benin “voudoun music”, influences from neighbouring countries, echoes of African military bands and European brass bands. Denagan Janvier Honfo’s voodoo-based percussion music blends traditional percussion with vocal polyphonies and later with European brasses. Angélique Kidjo’s cross-genre work combines soul, R&B, funk-rock, Caribbean styles, Brazilian, Cuban and other genres with Beninois rhythms like Gogbahoun and Fon lyrics. REGGAE – Yaya Yaovi launches a reggae group after visiting Bob Marley’s Tuff Gong studio. RAP and Afro-rap with French lyrics. Ardiess Posse and H2O innovate by rapping in Fon and adapt voodoo rhythms to socially engaged rap. K-Sim’s fusion draws on soul, JAZZ and HIP-HOP and uses traditional instruments and rhythms from Sahel cultures (mostly FULANI). Other musicians: Ignacio Blazio Osho & Orchestra Las Ondas, G.G. Vikey, L'Orchestre Black Santiago – founded in 1966 by Ignace de Souza, Honoré Avolonto, Orchestre Les Volcans Du Benin, Ambroise Akoha, Bluecky d’Almeida, Vivi l’Internationale, John Arcadius, Bobo We, Vano Baby.

search.title: Burkina Faso
search.text: Burkina Faso is explicitly listed among West African countries in the savanna/forest belt, situating it within the larger Sahel–Guinea savanna context of agricultural development and north–south migration.Voltaic cluster peoples (Mossi-Bariba, Senufo, Dogon, Kasena-Nankani, LoDagaa) are dispersed within Burkina Faso and neighboring states, so many of the region’s political and social histories (kingdoms, confederacies, secret societies, chieftaincies) are shared across current borders. Is described as a country of about sixty ethnic groups, with west and southwest under the influence of Mande culture shared with Mali and Côte d’Ivoire; DYULA people have their capital at Bobo-Dioulasso, a strategic commercial and cultural center whose strongest traditions are those of balafon and percussion. Central Burkina is inhabited mainly by Mossi (about half the population); the north is home to Fulbe (Fula/Peul), Bella and Touareg (linked to Mali and Niger); the south, along borders with Côte d’Ivoire, Benin and Ghana, includes Dyula, Senoufo, Gourounsi, Bissa, and Nankana peoples, all with strong musical traditions. Regional BALAFON and percussion-based traditional musics dominate west and southwest Burkina Faso, within the broader Mande cultural sphere shared with Mali and Côte d’Ivoire. 1950s regional orchestras play foxtrots, waltzes and tangos specifically for colonial administrators, signalling strong European dance influence that offer Dyula musicians a different kind of ensemble music alongside jaliyaa and dance drumming. 1970s Volta Jazz, Cheikh Lô, - The 1984 revolution of Thomas Sankara renames the country from Upper Volta to Burkina Faso, a political turning point explicitly linked to the redefinition of national identity in discussions of cultural diversity. Field-recording albums such as “Burkina Faso - Bisa, Gan, Lobi, Mossi, Savannah Rhythms, La Voix Des Peuls” and “Rhythms of the Grasslands” document representative traditional musics of major ethnic groups. *****Numerous musicians continue Mossi traditions for primarily Mossi audiences; Zoubna Zanda can fill a stadium without publicity, showing the strength of local celebrity within ethnic communities. An earlier generation of popular artists like Maurice Semporé, Oger Kaboré, Georges Ouédraogo, Tall Mountaga and Black So Man is noted for rich output but limited recognition outside Burkina Faso, marking a cohort whose fame remains largely domestic. Veteran singer-songwriter Gabin Dabiré, based in Italy since the mid-1970s, gains recognition for GUITAR based songs and complex choral arrangements, extending Burkinabé song into European world-music circuits. - Mid-1980s onward: groups like Farafina, Badenya Les Frères Coulibaly, Djiguiya, Kady Diarra and Sabouyouma begin touring Europe and America, inserting Burkinabé ensemble music and balafon tradition into international circuits. 1989: Bazar Music, founded by Kaboré Moussa, pioneers the local recording industry focused on traditional music; labels such as Sika Sound, Africa Musique and Faso Ambiance follow, making traditional music available on cassette and later CD. - 1996: Nuits Atypiques, a non-competitive international festival mixing traditional and modern acts, is launched in Koudougou by Koudbi Koala (founder of dance/percussion La Troupe Saaba) with support from French and Dutch world-music festivals. Burkinabé musicians like Zêdess, Jean Claude Bamogo and Solo Dja Kabako record some REGGAE alongside other genres. The compilation “Le Gang Rebel du Faso” features young artists such as Jah Verity, Razo Star, Terry Yiriban, Founy Faya (African-style SKA) Awa Melone (easy-listening), Sana Bob, Z. Mo, (tradi-moderne blends) and Les Sœurs Doga (purely traditional music). RAP / HIP-HOP becomes the most popular youth genre; the Ouaga Hip Hop Festival and media support foster an energetic local scene, and Ouagadougou is described as one of West Africa’s major trendsetters in hip-hop. Hip-hop artists such as Yeleen, Smockey, Sofaa, Kas Boven, Kouman Kan, Tere Pirattack and especially Faso Kombat become stars of the media-backed rap scene. Madson Junior, a ten-year-old rapper, wins the “Most Promising African Artist” award at the 2004 Kora Music Awards Bil Aka Kora’s “djongo music” fuses Kassena rhythms from the Gurunsi with modern arrangements that explicitly incorporate reggae and jazz influences, framed as original and sophisticated. Tim Winsé, initially a dancer in international troupes, turns to music to promote the Samo lolo musical bow, singing with modern instrumental accompaniment. Wuzzi (a group) win several awards at Semaine Nationale de la Culture; Sami Rama, a Bissa singer born in Côte d’Ivoire, pursues an international career after winning the 2002 Kundé d’Or Best Singer award. Amadou Balaké enhances his international profile and represents Burkina Faso within pan-African salsa by joining Africando All Stars in 2000. Urban dance preferences in Ouagadougou move through successive imported styles: Congolese ndombolo (from Congo), followed by Ivorian mapouka, and then coupé-décalé, which spawns a synthesizer-based style and a rapid succession of DJ-produced hits that gradually displace live bands in the maquis (open-air bar-restaurants).

search.title: Côte d’Ivoire
search.text: Côte d’Ivoire lies across both savanna and forest zones: northern regions in the Voltaic savanna belt; central and southern regions in the forest belt. The Bandama River within Côte d’Ivoire marks a long-term internal cultural boundary between two forest-music regions. The forest belt in general is marked by extreme ethnic fragmentation, small-scale political linkages, strong role of secret societies and age-grade associations. Regional traditional genres – Baoulé vocal polyphony, Guro "Zaouli" dance and Bete music, gbégbé and masked-dance repertoires (centre); Lobi (Dagaaba) xylophone traditions (northeast), Senoufo initiation/funeral music (north, including poro rhythms), Dan "Ge"mask music and genres like tan “dance song”, also meaning instrumental music/dance, zlee “praise song”, and gbo “funeral lament” (west), and Nzema/Appollo abissa drum-dance traditions (southeast coast) are presented as ongoing, distinctive musical cultures in Côte d’Ivoire. Tankë ge (“dance ge”) within the broader DAN GE institution perform at harvest celebrations and rites of passage such as weddings and funerals; their music and mask dances are documented in early 1960s recordings. Abidjan develops as the capital of West Africa’s recording industry and, through the 1970s, as the “musical crossroads” of the region, attracting artists from across the continent. “Wave of independence” in the 1960s; with Côte d’Ivoire newly independent, BAULE vocal pop built on the gbégbé rhythm artists like Les Soeurs Comöe are heard from transistor radios in every bar. Orchestre de la R.T.I. pop (with singers like Aïcha Koné and Nayanka Bell) blends Ivorian song with influences such as American soul and soft funk. Amédée Pierre’s dopé style uses a strong Congolese rumba flavour and becomes a model for later modern styles. Mamadou Doumbia – 1960s celebrity who tours throughout West Africa and the US; The 1970s and first 1980s remain a “heady period” for Abidjan’s scene. Ernesto DjéDjé’s ZIGLIBITHY (BETE rhythm base plus contemporary band set-up of drum kit, bass, guitars, horns, backing vocals) is hailed as giving Côte d’Ivoire its first modern musical identity; album “Gnoantre-Ziboté” (1977, recorded in Nigeria) becomes a pan-African hit. Gnaore Djimi’s polihet and Luckson Padaud’s laba laba derive directly from ziglibithy while keeping its traditional Bété spirit. Bailly Spinto – veteran of the local scene who continues to perform modern music strongly rooted in gbégbé. Anoman Brouh Félix, François Lougah and composer Jimmy Hyacinthe (modernizer traditional goly rhythm and producer for Aïcha Koné) are cited as enduring figures from the first generation of modern Ivorian artists. Audio Rama Orchestra, Sery Simplice, Ble Marcel Dibaga, Blissi Tebil, Justin Stanislas, Daouda, Meiway – Nzema/Appollo musician steeped in Grand-Bassam folk bands; after early success with Les Génitaux, moves to Paris, forms Défense d’Ivoire (prize-winning in 1987) and records “Ayibebou” (1989) with the beginnings of ZOBLAZO style. From the mid-1980s major labels (Ebony, DC Productions, SID, SACODIS) and big distributors withdraw one by one, reducing Côte d’Ivoire’s role as regional epicenter as studios open in neighboring countries and other markets grow. REGGAE “heralded” by Ivorian artists Alpha Blondy: is the first on the African scene to use reggae to speak to African urban youth, recording with The Wailers at Tuff Gong in Jamaica and launching a powerful West African reggae movement.Dickaël Liadé creator of Vava music modernizing Bété music. From 1987 to 1999, the revived ge "Gedro" from Dan village Petit Gbapleu performs constantly around Man, across Côte d’Ivoire and abroad, while dance masks are hired for religious practice, entertainment, and political/economical public-relations events. Petit Gbapleu Gedro group and associates – including Semlen Aimé (whose dream-inspired revival of Gedro in 1987 leads to a popular touring ge until Aimé’s death in 1999), master drummer Goueu Tia Jean-Claude (a young but highly sought-after drummer), elder singer Goneti, and organizer Gba Gama (Président des jeunes). Tiken Jah Fakoly (DYULA, forced to flee Côte d’Ivoire and settles in Bamako), together with Ismaël Isaac and Serges Kassy, follows on the reggae scene. ZOUGLOU – emerges in the early 1990s with the unrivaled leader Didier Bilé amid a university housing crisis in Yopougon; a satirical, ironic dance music with humorous lyrics exposing student hardship, mixing French, pidgin and Baoulé into a new slang, and functioning as protest music for Ivorian youth. It spreads to Burkina Faso and Mali and peaks in the mid-1990s; later leading bands include Magic System, Les Garagistes, Les Poussins Chocs and Soum Bill. From mid-1990s, hip-hop grows among youth and producers begin recording artists such as All Mighty, Angelo and RAS. December 1999 coup that ended almost forty years of continuous PDCI rule. Outbreak of war in September 2002 is described as the “death knell” of the Ivorian music industry; producers estimate 60–70 percent loss of market share and around 80 percent of national recordings being pirated. Mapouka – the style that overtook zouglou before coupé-décalé took over, indicating another major dance/music craze in the same era. Coupé-décalé – bursts onto the scene in a war-torn Côte d’Ivoire; in street-kid Noushi slang the term means “get rich quick and run.” It emerges in Paris clubs around 2000 (DJ Jacob at the Nelson) and spreads to other black nightclubs; from 2003, after Douk Saga’s hit “Sagacité,” it becomes massively popular across West Africa and grows to an estimated 40% of Ivorian musical output. Other notable coupé-décalé DJs include DJ Kaloudji (Abidjan), Serpent Noir, DJ Arafat, Innocent Versace and the Résistance DJ collective. Dobet Gnahoré’s 2004 “Ano Néko” blends urban and traditional textures (electric & acoustic instruments, gourds, balafon, aoko, bells, percussion) with socially engaged lyrics. Ahiwo Orchestra, N'Guess Bon Sens,

search.title: Gambia
search.text: Oral narratives in the Gambian jali tradition divide history into two periods: (1) the time of Sunjata and the formation of Mali (1200s) and (2) the time of the last mansas (kings; 1800s), showing that the memory of Mali’s monarchy extends into the nineteenth century. University teaching abroad: Jali Nyama Suso’s pioneering KORA classes at the University of Washington in 1971 open a path for Mande. Aesthetic ideals emphasise vocal power, courage before crowds, emotional impact and clear, truthful texts (as articulated by Gambian jali muso Nyulo Jebateh) Griot Muhamadou Salieu Suso. Transnational collaborations: projects linking Gambian kora player Foday Musa Suso with Mandingo Griots Society, the Kronos Quartet and Herbie Hancock demonstrate foreign partnerships that help define contemporary MANDE identity. Band Super Eagles rules 60s senegambian music scene and later grows out Ifang Bondi (Gambian band) noted as influencing Senegalese MBALAX. Anglo-African jali muso Sonah Jobarteh: her Anglo-African identity and kora virtuosity embody a transnational model of female jali

search.title: Ghana
search.text: Ghana is described as a British colony on Africa’s “Gold Coast”, situated within a West African region heavily affected by the Atlantic slave trade during the broader colonial period (early 1500s–late 1800s). Colonial Gold Coast society with elite “high-class, top-hat-and-tails” dance evenings, where local ballroom and RAGTIME bands ***(Excelsior Orchestra, Jazz Kings of Accra, Accra Orchestra, Cape Coast Sugar Babies) entertained the Ghanaian elite in clubs and dance halls. After 1870, stationing of West Indian colonial soldiers in Cape Coast and Elmina and their Afro-Caribbean music inspired coastal Ghanaian musicians, portrayed as innovators who first refashion regimental, classical, theatrical and church musics, than spread theese through southern Ghana. Early HIGHLIFE emerges from combining local idioms and rhythms like FANTE Osibisaaba and ADAHA brass-band music with KRU GUITAR styles from Liberia, ASIKO music from Sierra Leone, European church music, military brass-band music and sea shanties in the ports and coastal towns. --- Early twentieth century --- The term “highlife” is coined for the fashionable elite dance evenings, marking a named urban dance culture under colonial rule. Kwame Asare (Jacob Sam), pioneer highlife guitarist who learned from a Kru sailor in the 1920s, and his Kumasi Trio, made the first highlife recordings in London in 1928. Since 1930s, recording industry connects Ghana to London (Zonophone, HMV, Parlophone), with Ghanaian musicians travelling to record, embedding Ghana in early transnational music circuits. PALM-WINE music: early twentieth-century dockside and bar music combining local West African instruments with portable instruments of visiting seamen (CONCERTINA, HARMONICA, GUITAR). George William Aingo was one of the most famous early Fante palm-wine guitarists. As palm wine moves inland, it absorbs features of the AKAN SEPREWA (harp-lute), creating the more “rootsy” ODONSON or Akan “BLUES” style, recorded by early guitarists/vocalists like Appiah Adjekum, Kwame Mireku, Kwesi Pepera, Osei Bonsu, Kwesi Menu and Kamkan. CONCERT-PARTY: local VAUDEVILLE / MUSIC-HALL format for elites with tap-dancing, ragtime and short comic sketches in English, drawing on American blackface performance. Fanti comedian Bob Johnson takes the concert party away from urban elites into the “rural hinterland”, starting its indigenization and linking it to Akan storytelling traditions and folklore. KONKOMBA marching bands arise in 1930s Akan towns and villages that cannot afford brass instruments, using local drums and voices instead. ***Husunu Adonu Afadi-Ladzekpo – son of Kofi Zate and leader-poet/composer for the Yevavo Axatsewu Club, which formed in the late 1930s; his songs are preserved in Lasibi’s repertory, showing intergenerational transmission. --- 1940s–50s --- During WWII, presence of thousands of British and American servicemen introduces SWING and JAZZ into Ghana’s urban music, providing audiences and influences for bands that later become highlife dance bands. Servicemen Bob Vans fighting in Burma (Myanmar) run concert-parties for troops, then returned and found the group Burma Jokers and later the Ghana Trio, linking wartime experience to post-war popular theatre and nationalist politics. After WWII, E.T. Mensah & His Tempos Band initiate a professional highlife dance-band movement: big-band urban dance music enriched with swing, jazz, AFRO-CUBAN percussion and CALYPSO. Guy Warren (Kofi Ghanaba), master drummer and early Tempos' member, introduced Afro-Cuban percussion into highlife and later moved to the US recording seminal Afro-jazz albums. King Bruce, jazz and swing loving trumpeter, founded multiple bands like Black Beats and Barbecues de Ghana. Led by E.K. Nyame (key figure trained with Appiah Adjekum), guitar-band highlife evolves from palm-wine groups and expands using dance-band instruments. Comic highlife opera emerges when Nyame’s Akan Trio attaches a concert-party to his guitar-band, a model adopted widely by 1950s guitar-bands like I.E. Mason, Kwaa Mensah, Kwabena Nyama, Uhuru Dance Band, Kakaiku, Yamoah, T.O. "Jazz" Ampoumah, Jaguar Jokers, Bob Cole, Onyina’s Royal Trio and Dr. Gyasi’s Noble Kings, touring villages and performing acoustic and early electric highlife tied to popular theatre. After independence in 1957, Kwame Nkrumah’s socialist-aligned government promotes indigenous music, funds professional performing-arts troupes and Workers Brigade concert-parties, and travels with full dance bands as part of his political entourage. Bob Ansah was a concert-party leader whose group supported the nationalist cause. Rising nationalist struggle, rapid urbanization and social change provide fertile ground for classic highlife of the 1950s–60s, that becomes Ghana’s “urban dance music”, with original songs in English and local languages, incorporating traditional rhythms into modern arrangements and sometimes venturing into Congo music and calypso. --- 1960s–1970s --- the “Golden Era” of Ghanaian music, focusing largely on Accra, the capital. Ghanaian music absorbs Congolese music, POP and especially SOUL, whose “black and proud” ethos and fashions encourage experimentation. Jerry Hansen – Leader of the Ramblers International Dance Band (formed 1962), whose fully professional fifteen-man line-up sustained a living from shows and records for nearly twenty years. KPANLOGO drum-dance, created in early 1960s by Otoo Lincoln, Frank Lane and Okule Foes, becomes a key GA recreational rhythm later revived and internationally popular. Mustapha Tettey Addy also helped create kpanlogo and later formed the Obonu Drummers. In early 1970s, Afro-rock, AFRO-BEAT and Afro-funk appear in Ghana with bands like Psychedelic Aliens, Big Beats, Boombaya, Sawaaba Soundz, African Brothers International Band and Osibisa (London based). Afro-roots fusion groups such as Hedzoleh Soundz, Basa Basa Soundz and the Bunzus Band dig into Ghanaian culture and present it in sophisticated fusion packages. Mac Tontoh (Osibisa) later formed Kete Warriors. Koo Nimo – Folk guitarist who learned palm-wine techniques from Kwame Asare, Kwaa Mensah and E.K. Nyame, later adding CLASSICAL-GUITAR, European and American jazz influences; leads the acoustic Adadam Agoromma Group. Nii Tei Ashitey and Wulomei, leaders of the Ga cultural revival, encourage youth “to forget foreign music and do their own thing”. Other Ga cultural troupes like Bukom, Dzadzeloi, Blemabii Band, Abladei Culture Group, Ashiedu Keteke and Suku Troupe promote “rootsy” Ga music. Back-to-roots acoustic palm-wine returns as some guitar-band veterans (Kwaa Mensah, T.O. “Jazz” Ampoumah, Kwabena Nyama) move back from electric to acoustic formats. DAGBAMBA drummer Abubakari Lunna works as a professional with the Ghana National Folkloric Company, retires from government service in 1988, then returns to northern Ghana to serve in the Dagbon courtly system until his father’s death. Lunna’s life story underlines the contrast between “the north” and “the south” of Ghana. In late 70s, the Anya Agbekor Society illustrates urban working-class Ghanaian contexts for EWE music in Accra, with musicians like Godwin Agbeli, Evans Amenumey, Gideon Foli Alorwoyie and Dogbevi Abaglo. The Gambian KORA player Foday Musa Suso met Adam Rudolph in Ghana; together they formed the Mandingo Griots Society, basically a rock band with the kora out front, showing Ghana as a meeting place for transnational, experimental ensembles. -- From late 1970s, dance-band highlife declines amid new imported pop. Due to economical crisis, maintaining large full-time bands becomes “near impossible” as clubs and dance halls close and equipment breaks down. Many musicians emigrate to Europe and North America and, within Afro-pop “world music,” Ghana contributes the enduring highlife genre and joins Nigeria and South Africa in dominating African music exports: in Britain, highlife and Ghanaian forms through artists like Kwabena Oduro-Kwarteng, Kofi Adu, Herman Asafo-Agyei, Sam Ashley, Alfred “Kari” Bannerman, Jon Kay and Ben Brako, added African elements to the 1980s “world music” boom and feeded into bands such as Hi-Life International, Orchestre Jazira, Kabbala and Dade Krama; in Germany, highlife fused with funk and rock to produce a harder-edged studio BURGER-HIGHLIFE electronic sound, beginning with George Darko’s “Akoo Te Brafo” and continuing with Kantata, Daddy Lumba and Nana Acheampong, producing dancefloor-oriented disco/highlife hybrids popular at home; Pat Thomas, A.B. Crentsil (Ahenfo Band), Jewel Ackah and Herman Asafo-Agyei moved to or recorded in Canada and U.S.A.; other diaspora-linked musicians: Sloopy Mike Gyanfi, Obo Addy, Andy Vans, Nana Tsiboe, Afro Moses, Okyeame Asante, Bob Pinado, Eddie Omensah. In Nigeria, during its oil boom, Ghanaian highlife bands like Okukuseku, The Canadoes, Opambuas, Odoywewu, Kuul Strangers, Golden Boys, Citystyle and Beach Scorpions (often one-off albums) flourish particularly in Lagos and IGBO regions. At home, by the early 1980s only two studios survive and cassette piracy spreads, prompting musicians to organize and lobby for government copyright protection and anti-piracy laws. Field recordings such as the Odo ye few korye kuw Vocal Band in the Fante area (Abura Tuakwa, Ghana, 1984) document village-based ensembles. GOSPEL-HIGHLIFE: numerous Pentecostal/evangelical groups like Genesis Gospel Singers and Christo Asafo Mission, and female stars like Helen Rhabbles, Mary Ghansah, Diana Akiwumi, Tagoe Sisters and Daughters of Glorious Jesus play variants of highlife, making gospel a dominant commercial style, with around 60% of commercial pop output by the 1990s and with many churches running their own studios. REGGAE and reggae-highlife gain strong followings with Kojo Antwi’s soft reggae in TWI, K.K. Kabobo’s reggae highlife, Rocky Dawuni, and especially Amekye Dede’s reggae-highlife idiom. Filmmaker and musician Ahmed Adam popularizes the INDIAN-STYLE/LINE, a music sub-genre in Tamale heavily influenced by BOLLYWOOD musicals; in the mid-1990s, some rhythms and melodies are direct replicas of particular Bollywood songs, with Dagbanli lyrics substituted; Memunatu Lardi, Alfa Tuferu and Sherifatu Issah evolve beyond direct covers to create original melodies and rhythms. Continued classical highlife output ranges from acoustic palm-wine to electric guitar bands with groups and artists like African Heroes, Amekye Dede, Alex Konadu, Alpha Waves, Gold Coasters, Western Diamonds, J.A. Adofo’s City Boys, Teacher and his Afrikana, Ebo Taylor, Gyedu Blay-Ambolley, Nana Tuffour, Felix Owusu, Megastar Band, Nakorex and it's artits solo projects Nat “Amandzeba” Brew, Akosua Agyepong and Rex Omar. The Smithsonian Folkways release “Rhythms of Life, Songs of Wisdom: Akan Music from Ghana, West Africa (1996)” presents Akan musics, including talking drums and vocal bands, to global audiences. New roots-fusion musicians and ensembles like Afrikan Show Boys, Atongo Zimba, Aaron Bebe Sukura, King Ayisoba, Hewale Sounds, Pan African Orchestra, Agorsor Cultural Ensemble, Takashi, Wassa Afrika, Selorm Cultural Troupe, Osei Korankye, “Oscarmore” Ofori, Stan Plange, Atongo Zimba and Captain Yaba blend traditional rhythms and instruments like ATENTEBEN flute and northern Ghanaian XALAM (MOLO or KOLIKO) lutes with contemporary song forms. -- Mid-1990s: HIP-LIFE (hip-hop highlife) emerges as an urban youth genre, with lyrics in Twi and Ga and imagery drawn from U.S.A. RAP culture, giving city youth an “artistic voice”, with musicans like Reggie Rockstone, Nana King, Daasebre, Lord Kenya, Akatakyie, Nana Quame, Native Funk Lords, Tic Tac, Ex Doe & Chicago, Terry Bonchaka, Buk-Bak, Castro, Adane Best, Omanhene Pozo, Obour, Okonfo Kwade and Sydney. Southern Ghana’s Akan culture dominates Ghana’s popular culture, especially in hiplife, highlife and hip-hop, whose lyrics focus heavily on Akan language and culture, while media from marginalized northern ethnic groups is relegated to the periphery. Despite marginalization, Northern Ghanaian artists produce music addressing social, political, economic and cultural themes for local audiences, blending Dagbanli language and Dagbamba cultural elements (proverbs, wise sayings, rhythmic and melodic patterns, values and analogies) with “Afro-American and Western-inspired idioms,” giving rise to what observers call a self-authenticated “Hybrid Pop Identity”. Prince Mahama, an early contemporary pop instrumentalist and blind musician from Tamale, teaches guitar to younger artists, including Sheriff Ghale. Hiplife artists in Tamale like Lil-K, Deensi, Don Sigli, Fancy Gadam, Maccasio and Lord Destro produce mixtapes by downloading popular instrumentals from the internet and rewriting them with their own lyrics, often in Dagbanli, integrating global beats into local narratives (global pop via internet-enabled remix culture). Kassim Gazor, described as one of the pioneering contemporary music artists in Tamale, is a non-literate “musical griot” who composes and “writes” songs in his mind, records ideas on his mobile phone, and later develops them in the studio, demonstrating a complex oral–digital creative process. Other artists from Northern Ghana: Abu Sadiq, Prince Okla, “7 in 1 for Peace” Collective, Optional King. In recent years, a Kpanlogo derived dance called AZONTO becomes widely popular across Ghana, spreads outside the country and appears in Afro-pop music videos. ***Neotraditional drum dances like Ga kpanlogo and Ewe borborbor are taught alongside older traditions, indicating a continuing process of innovation within “tradition”.

search.title: Guinea Bissau
search.text: More than three centuries of Portuguese domination leave almost no formal musical heritage beyond backyard and ceremonial music. Jaliyaa is framed as a “classical” tradition of the Mande. In the early 1930s, ethnomusicologist George Herzog undertakes one of the first detailed studies of performance in the Guinea Coast area. 'backyard beats' centre on Gumbay and related KRIOL styles (tina, tinga) as well as ethnic forms such as KUSSUNDE and brosca/broxa (BALANTA), djambadon (Mandinga) and kundere (Bijagos), all closely tied to funerals, spirit-calling, initiation and harvest rituals. A long liberation struggle culminates in independence in the mid-1970s; Kriolu music becomes central to mobilizing and uniting the population. José Carlos Schwarz's and Aliu Bari's Le Cobiana Djazz's Kriolu music is taken up as mother of all contemporary GB bands, defining GUMBE as a new national genre as a mixture of traditional musics, helping defining indipendence. In 1973 Ernesto Dabό (later Djôrçon) records "M’Ba Bolama", a gumbe-style Kriolu song and first modern Guinea Bissau single. Super Mama Djombo's music mixes gumbe with more sophisticated band arrangements and electric guitar. The 1980s are marked by deep economic crisis: shops are almost empty and there is a chronic lack of food; songs move from revolutionary optimism toward social and political critique, and some singers are jailed or banned. Socially engaged solo records by José Carlos Schwarz, Sidonio Quaresma and Ramiro Naka retain narrative lyricism while adapting to faster disco-type dance grooves; Zé Manel, drummer with Super Mama Djombo records the album 'Tustumunhus di Aonti' (1983) with strong political lyrics and is banned from public performance. Justino Delgado becomes popular after being jailed for sarcastic songs about President Nino Vieira. Salvador Embaló Tchando spends two years in jail before emigrating. Kaba Mané’s work is described as a modern kussundé style with kora-like electric guitar. In the 1990s, Guinea-Bissau enters a phase described as 'Survival and War': IMF-backed liberalization yields little improvement, even as clubs and discos multiply in Bissau; bands such as Tabanka Djaz and Maio Coope & Gumbezarte achieve the first significant commercial breakthroughs, offering an exciting Kriolu mix that incorporates various ethnic styles while remaining constrained by limited recording resources, while Manecas Costa’s work foregrounds gumbe rhythms in refined acoustic settings that address hunger, corruption and suffering. A civil war in 1998–99 devastates the city, destroying venues and bands. In post-war Guinea-Bissau, many bands have disintegrated and numerous musicians live in exile; gumbe remains the rhythmic backbone of club and radio playlists, even as other African dance genres, Stevie Wonder-style soul and salsa share the space, with artists like Guto Pires and Nino Galissa. Bidinte blends West African, Euro-Arabian and flamenco elements with Kriolu lyrics.

search.title: Guinea Conakry
search.text: Guinea is structured into four historically interconnected though culturally distinct regions: Basse Côte, Futa Jallon, Haute Guinée, Guinée Forestière JALIYAA is framed as a “classical” tradition of the Mande. Early 20th-century Guinean urban culture sees the GUITAR introduced (probably by soldiers returning from Europe after World War I), becoming a symbol of modernity and replacing the BANJO in Conakry ballroom bands. In the early 1930s, ethnomusicologist George Herzog undertakes one of the first detailed studies of performance in the Guinea Coast area recorded in wax cylinders. 1950 high-fidelity recordings of MANINKA music from Guinea document early-20th-century forms of MANDE classical music. Keita Fodeba founds the troupe Les Ballets Africains in Paris in the 1950s, later directed by Kante Facelli. Conakry orchestras such as La Douce Parisette and La Joviale Symphonie serve colonial elites with European and Latin American dances (beguine, waltz, tango, paso doble) plus a few 'Guinean folk' pieces. Guinea’s independence (1958) turns Les Ballets Africains into a national ensemble, and every nation where the Mande live establishes a similar state-sponsored group. Its 1959 New York debut and later status as Guinea’s national ensemble model how “national” Mande culture can be staged for Western audiences and inspire similar troupes in countries where Mande live. Syli Orchestre National, Bembeya Jazz National, Balla et ses Balladins and Keletigui et ses Tambourinis develop a big-band style rooted in Cuban, Latin and Mande jeli repertoire, with musicians like Grand Papa Diabaté, Sekou Bembeya Diabate and Demba Camara . Women play enduring roles in handing down jalyaa, from Les Amazones de Guinée and female jeli stars like Kadé Diawara and Mama Kanté. Kouyate Sory Kandia, star vocalist from Les Ballets Africains, combines an operatic tenor range with a griot timbre. El Hadj Djeli Sory Kouyaté, a virtuoso balafonist and leader of the Ensemble Concoba, epitomises classical jeli balafon repertoire and virtuosity. Kulung and the Woni Ensemble are recorded transmitting KPELLE traditions. In the first 70s Kante Manfila moves to Mali to join Les Ambassadeurs du Motel de Bamako; same for Mory Kanté, joining the Rail Band. M’Bady et Diaryatou Kouyaté, KORA player and singer couple featured on “Guinée: kora et chant du N’Gabou”, representing leading Guinean exponents of jaliyaa. In 1984, Guinea's state arts system collapses; General Lansana Conté's regime pursues privatization, and music shifts into a free-market system dominated by private producers, piracy and bootlegging. Cassette-era Mande pop develops a vedette-centred format: star singers and state-orchestra veterans like Mama Kanté, Kadé Diawara, Kerfala Kanté and Mory Djely Kouyate are backed by synthetic textures instead of large live orchestras, recasting jeliya in romantic, highly produced pop formats. Sekouba Bambino, a jeli from Mali and former Bembeya Jazz singer, becomes Guinea’s most revered vedette. Female jeli like Oumou Dioubaté, Missia Saran Diabate, Sayon Bamba Camara and Maciré Sylla continue jalyaa traditions and fusions. In 1987, Mory Kanté moves into hi-tech global dance music with his 1987 hit song "Yé Ké Yé Ké", which was one of Africa's best-ever selling hits. Ibro Diabaté’s Paris-produced debut album 'Allah Nana' (early 1990s) is widely praised for its delicate arrangements. Djeli Moussa Diawara. A hybrid style labelled 'Mande-zouk' emerges in Guinea, blending Antillean zouk beats with local rhythms; artist Fode Baro becomes one of its key exponents. Late 1990s and early 2000s bring diversification beyond Mande jeli dominance: while some veterans plan institutions such as Mory Kanté, diversified scenes arise. Fula semi-acoustic pop emphasises flutes and local rhythms: Lama Sidibé becomes a national Fula star with 'Faalaama' (1999), built on thorough research into Futa Jallon traditions; Petit Yero Bantinghel, Binta Laly Sow and Fatou Barry adapt trimmed-down nyamakala (fula jeli) sounds into accessible contemporary pop. Les Espoirs de Coronthie SUSU 'busker pop' turns the rattling of street instruments into chart hits. Diasporic Afro-jazz and roots-pop projects rework Guinean traditions, as in Momo Wandel Soumah’s Afro-Swing, Ba Cissoko’s kora-rock and Maciré Sylla’s jazzy Sussu/Mande fusions. Hip-hop and reggae figures such as Kill Point (seen as godfathers of the scene), Ideal Black Girls and Degg J Force 3 develop Guinean rap, often recording in Dakar’s more advanced studios; Bill de Sam’s rap version of the classic 'Sunjata' unexpectedly gains international airplay.

search.title: Liberia
search.text: Present-day residents migrated from the grassland area of the former Mali kingdom down to the coastal area between the 1500s and 1800s. Mande-speaking groups (including Kpelle, Vai, Loma, Belle, Gbandi, Gio, Dan, etc.) are said to have had the most dramatic impact on the Western Forest subregion.Mende institutions of Poro and warfare are seen as key conveyors of influence to Gola and, via Gola, to Vai and Dei. Kwa speakers live in Liberia (Dei, Bassa, Gbi, Kran, Padebu, Kru, Grebo, Jabo); the Kwa in Liberia have felt heavy influence from migrants who have become dominant in the region. Tukulor, Fulɓe, Wolof, Serer, and Jola (Senegambians) related peoples have migrated to Sierra Leone and Liberia, adding West Atlantic elements to the Liberian population. Migrations from the north continuing until the 1800s resulted in the invention of an indigenous alphabet among the VAI and in the secret societies Poro and Sande, described as vehicles for the transmission of culture from one generation to the next in the Western Forest area that includes Liberia. Early 19th-c. slave owners and idealistic African American missionaries in the US create the American Colonization Company to establish a colony in West Africa and “send black Americans back” while “civilizing” local Africans, just before the American Civil War. The colony is set up in 1822 and becomes Liberia (“free country”) in 1847. The African American settlers (“Americo-Liberians”) quickly form an elite whose culture clashes with that of local populations and who, for a time, trade people from the interior as slaves. This settler elite dominates politics after independence, forming the background against which later musical developments unfold. Indigenous rituals, Christianity and Islam coexist. Church choir music is introduced by settler ministers in the nineteenth century and becomes a key Liberian style. Lower-class coastal KRU sailors communities formed the social base for PALM-WINE guitar-based dance and entertainment musics (syncretic fusion of European, Caribbean, Afro-American, and indigenous West African elements) performed informally in seaport taverns in the early twentieth century (prototypical HIGHLIFE genre). “Palm-wine highlife” groups proliferated from the 1930s to the early 1950s, extending this style inland and into minstrel and dramatic troupes. Early 1930s wax-cylinder recordings of music on the southeastern coast made by George Herzog. The 1950s mark the first recordings of Liberian singers, still in a relatively stable pre-war political climate. A secular choral movement emerges in the 1950s (?40s?) with The Greenwood Singers, paralleling the long-established religious choirs rooted in the settler churches. Blind pianist Howard B. Hayes writes and plays catchy tunes in many idioms, including palm wine, calypso (Caribbean) and ragtime-like pieces. The 1954 recording "Songs of the African Coast: Café Music of Liberia and Ghana" mix calypso and ragtime-like rumbas with distinctly local parlance and humour, focusing on everyday life themes. In 1970s artists like Morris Dorley and his Sunset Boys and Anthony Senyon Nagbe help “kick-start a real African music scene” with songs rooted in local realities and indigenous languages. Army musicians Robert Toe and Jimmy Diggs record cassettes that mix local and international material. T. Kpan Nimely and Donald Cooper develop a hybrid sound that blends reggae and highlife with Afro-rock and “discolypso”, described as a disco/funk version of Sierra Leone’s popular MARINGA music. Gospel singer Hawa Daisy Moore starts her career, than joins Miriam Makeba's band. E. Tonieh Williams’s band Liberian Dream, with Zack Roberts and Gebah Swaray (Zack and Gebah), performs what they call “Afro-Disco Music”, adding another hybrid dance style. Afro-jazz band Kapingbdi, founded by Ebenezer Kojo Samuels, tours Africa, Europe and the US, representing a fusion of jazz and African idioms. 1972 album "Music of the Kpelle of Liberia" demonstrates KPELLE influence in the area. Princess Fatu Gayflor work bridges pre-war cultural performance and diaspora life. KingBlack Hayes released his first hit, "Don’t Play Foul", in 1989. ****Won-Ldy Paye, E. Kaikpai Paasewe & Princess Hawa Moore – contemporary musicians who incorporate elements of the old musics of ethnic groups such as the Vai (coast near Monrovia) and the forest-based Kpelle and Dan into modern styles; End of 1989, Charles Taylor enters Liberia with armed men, starting the first civil war and closing this pre-war musical phase; hundreds of thousands flee and many musicians, like Yatta Zoe, go into exile, and studios and radio stations are looted, destroyed and burned. Zack Roberts, SwaRay (Gebah & Maudline Swaray) and Miatta Fahnbulleh form a repertoire of anti-war, refugee-focused music. A second civil war (2000–03) pushes many prominent musicians abroad, deepening diaspora musical production. Gospel and choral traditions remain strong with groups like African Gospel a Cappella. Refugee rap/hip-hop emerges with The Boyz of Butuburam. Naser Sokay & Jake D move to the U.S.A.. After wars, local music starts “coming back”, increasingly drawing on Liberia’s interior, which had long been isolated. Musicians face heavy competition from US artists, ever-present reggae, mass-produced Congolese NDOMBOLO and the newer craze, ZOUGLOU from neighboring Côte d’Ivoire. Liberia is described as “cassette country”, and radio DJs help bring local tracks by artists like Zack Roberts and King O’Bryant.

search.title: Mali
search.text: Mali lies where Western Sudanic (Manding, Fulɓe, Soninke), Central Sudanic (Songhai, Fulani), and Voltaic (Senufo, Dogon, etc.) clusters intersect, so its territory participates in several regional musical systems. The broader West African savanna region that includes Mali is portrayed as a long-standing zone of intercultural communication linking north–south and east–west routes through the Sahara, Sahel and major rivers, providing the environmental and commercial framework for Mali’s musical and political history. Bazoumana Sissoko, “the old lion” from Segou, emerges as a blind BAMBARA style NGONI player and singer whose recordings become canonical. KORA masters like Djelimady Sissoko and Sidiki Diabaté are recognized leaders of the JALIYAA tradition. Mali gains independence from France in 1960; President Modibo Keita founded Ensemble Instrumental National Du Mali in 1961; its staged, multi-ethnic format becomes a prestige model influencing neighboring countries. District orchestras are formed in Bamako, giving young musicians their first moves away from purely traditional Mande music, fusing into into AFRO-CUBAN and JAZZ, with bands like Kélétigui Diabaté's Orchestre National "A" de la République du Mali, Las Maravillas de Mali and Le National Badema. *****Apollo sound (Afro-Cuban / sumu hybrid) – 1970s Apollo ensembles sit between acoustic sumu and Cuban-style dance bands, combining balafon with electric guitar and Afro-Cuban percussion (timbales, drumkit). A military coup in 1968 brings Moussa Traoré to power; he further encourages cultural authenticity and launches the Biennale Festival. Super Biton de Segou win the first Biennale (1970) and again in 1972 with Bamana rhythm-based styles transposed to horns and guitars, emblematic of this era’s “roots-dance-band” synthesis. From early independence onwards, female jelimuso singers like Ami Koïta, Kandia Kouyaté, Tata Bambo Kouyaté, Fanta Damba, Fanta Sacko, Naïny Diabaté and Bako Dagnon gain fame primarily through wedding parties, composing some of the most popular 20th-century jeli songs. Sorry Bamba and Orchestre Kanaga de Mopti. A distinctive set of popular music styles emerged in the Sudanic desert countries, especially Mali and Senegal. Before this, Congolese music and other imported forms tended to dominate dance repertoires in these regions. As demand for music in local languages grew, Mali and its neighbors developed their own popular genres, heavily influenced by the music of the griots. From 1950s moonlight village dances, Allata Broulaye develops the KAMALE-NGONI (youth harp). Late 1970s and early 1980s see bands in Abidjan and Paris like Tidiani Koné's Rail Band, Guinean guitarist Kante Manfila's Les Ambassadeurs du Motel de Bamako and Mory Kanté (famous in Mali but from Guinea Conakry) experimenting with more explicitly international pop sounds. The success of albums like Salif Keïta’s "Soro" fuels a broader “World Music” boom for Malian artists. Ali Farka Touré (SONGHAI guitarist) is described as pointing to kinship with bluesmen of the Mississippi, positioning a widely circulating Mande GUITAR style within an American BLUES narrative, becoming known as DESERT-BLUES. TOUAREG band Tinariwen formed in Tamanrasset, developed ISHUMAR music in military camps in Libya set up by Colonel Ghaddafi to train young Tamashek men; during rebellion they became “pied pipers” of the rebel movement, galvanizing dispossessed youth living clandestinely in Algeria/Libya. Theyr guitarist Ibrahim Ag Alhabib is credited with inventing modern rock-generation Tamashek style known simply as guitar. In the 1980s and early 90s drought + rebellion drove many Tamashek into exile; Tartit formed in Mauritanian refugee camps during the bitterest years of the Touareg rebellion in the early 1990s and led by Fadimata Wallet Oumar. The Biennale ceases in 1988, the same year as a Touareg rebellion in northern Mali, marking a turning point from state festivals to new musical circuits. In 1991, student protests over bursaries escalate into a popular uprising; clashes with the army leave over a thousand dead. A military coup led by Amadou Toumani Touré follows, then a transition to democratic government in 1992 under President Alpha Oumar Konaré. Post-independence acoustic youth music evolves into urban WASSOULOU, based on the most ancient SUMU praise and wedding music tradition: it carries strong messages of social freedom and powerful dance rhythms, with young women singers as its main stars such as Oumou Sangaré, Nahawa Doumbia, Coumba Sidibe, Kagbé Sidibé, Sali Sidibé, Djeneba Diakité and later Fatoumata Diawara. Toumani Diabaté’s collaborations with many other improvising traditions generate hybrid styles whose formal logic is shared with jazz and other foreign idioms. Mande divas such as Mah Damba, Babani Koné and Rokia Traoré build reputations through arts organisations, radio, television and recording industries. Abdoulaye "Koutiala" Diabaté adapts Bamana folk dance rhythms to electric dance music. Lobi Traoré – Singer-guitarist from Bamako who mixes non-jeli Bamana style with “raw electric blues”. Amadou & Mariam – Blind blues-rock duo from Bougouni. Trend towards smaller semi-acoustic groups lead by artists like elder Djelimady Tounkara and Kassé Mady Diabaté and younger Habib Koité and Ballaké Sissoko draw on celebratory jeli wedding styles. Sékouba Bambino became a star in Guinea Conakry's jeli circuit. Boubacar Traoré. Issa Bagayogo’s remixes push kamale-ngoni sound towards techno-leaning dance music. Since the mid-1990s, urban youth embrace the BALAFON music of SENUFO people; Neba Solo modernizes balani by adding bass notes for a pronounced bass line, leading to BALANI-SHOW style. Les Escrocs RAP over live jeli-style bands; Tata Pound rap in Bamana over sampled hip-hop and reggae grooves, known for outspoken criticism of government; Ivorian reggae star Tiken Jah Fakoly, forced to flee Côte d’Ivoire, settles in Bamako and helps revive reggae among youth.
