Mamadou Diabate (kora player based in North Carolina) leads ensembles with balafon, string bass and drums, creatively rearranging traditional Mande songs into popular concert formats; Morikeba Kouyate and others do similar work abroad. Bassekou Kouyate, with his sons on ngoni variants and wife Amy Sacko as lead singer, represents a modern, family-based ensemble where hereditary ngoni playing meets contemporary staging and recording. Baba Salah, songhai. Hundreds of cassettes circulate, and festivals (2001, 2005) in Bamako celebrate this repertoire, whose similarities to gnawa and the blues are noted through figures such as Seydou Traoré, Amadou Sangaré, Sibiri Samaké and Yoro Sidibé.

search.title: Niger
search.text: Niger described as a huge landlocked nation merging with the Sahara to the north. Niger’s “diverse culture” described in terms of major regional groupings (Touareg north; Hausa centre/south; Beriberi east; Djerma/Songhai west; Dendi south).Wodaabe Fulani “gerewol” face-painted dancing and polyphonic singing ceremony for young men described as an important annual date on Niger’s calendar. Dendi described as using techniques/instruments from neighbouring Benin and Nigeria. Beriberi “beautiful polyphonic singing”. “Wonderful historical recordings” made made by french composer and ethnomusicologist Tolia Nikiprowetsky in Niger in 1963 with Songhai, Djerma, Hausa, Beriberi, Touareg and Fulani musicians. “Belluwel” and “akhaguwwen” singing techniques documented in recordings made 1973–1998 in northwest Niger (Azawagh region). Mystical chant “dhikr” documented around In Gall (recordings dated 1973–1998). “Sahel drought of 1973” described as leaving enduring hardship and halting Niger’s small recording output. In “strongly Muslim Niger,” music as entertainment “not readily accepted”; for many years after independence there was little cultural policy. Electronic Nigerien music from Mamman Sani. After the death of military dictator Seyni Kounché (1987), government looked to music to bring cultures together. Prix Dan Gourmou launched (cash prize + national youth-club tour), prompting music/dance ensembles, with some groups seek to add modern instruments to traditional ones. Alassane Dante (formerly director of the National Ballet; co-director of CCFN) among those who set up Prix Dan Gourmou. Abdallah Oumbadougou, beacon TOUAREG guitarist for ISHUMAR / DESERT-BLUES style, formed the band Takrist n'Akal and later participated in the international band Desert Rebelle. Mamane Barka (nomad of the Toubou tribe from north), Groupe Oyiwane (northern Niger collective) Centre for Musical Training and Promotion established for modern techniques/instruments; materialized 1990 via a six-year European Fund for Development grant. Takeda, leaded by guitarist Abdoulaye Alhassane Toure (Koudede) and formed with top CFPM musicians and singers: Yacouba Moumouni, Moussa Poussy (Djerma; grandson of a traditional healer), Adams Junior, Fati Mariko, John Sofakolé played MASA 1995 in Abidjan. Niamey described as having only two small studios (incl. CFPM) and only two tape-duplicating companies; musicians often self-produce cassettes, facing piracy. Saadou Bori (Hausa-speaker; practitioner of dango spirit music and trance-dancing). First RAP concert in Niamey at CCFN (1996). Nigerien rap follows the exiled Belgian-based group Tod One; early groups include Massacreur and Wassika (first to write lyrics in Hausa and Djerma). Lilwal (collective formed 2001) bringing together Black Daps, Djoro G, WassWong, Kaïdan Gaskia. Other Nigerien rappers: Sah Fonda, MTS Matassa, Metaphore Crew. Modern Nigerien group Mamar Kassey described as inspired by Fulani, Hausa, Songhai, and Djerma traditional music. Festival-driven “hip” attention to Touareg music “in recent years”; first Festival in the Desert (2001) referenced as a globalizing catalyst for Malian band Tinariwen and desert sounds, carrying “desert pride” message worldwide; 2003 festival recording described as a classic. Tidawt (from Agadez); Etran Finatawa: (four Touareg + six Wodaabe) trance-like rock guitars + driving percussion + chanting; songs about healing, herding cattle, camel racing; some built on calabash patterns with call-and-response vocals. Dangana (formed 2001 in Zinder) highlighted for forging a new sound via terracotta jars and a hybrid rock-like approach. Radio Ténéré’s support for Lakal Kaney. Harouna Goge described as a virtuoso of the one-stringed goge fiddle (following his father, though against his wishes); performs Dendi-country songs (mostly spirit invocations). Mdou Moctar described as the "Hendrix of the Sahara". Bombino. Azna de L'Ader Touareg rock from the '80s, released in 2016. Etran de L’Aïr, Alhousseini Anivolla,

search.title: Nigeria
search.text: The region is presented as a tropical band where forest near the coast gives way to savannah inland and, at the northern fringe, the Sahara. Lagos repatriate communities (Sierra Leonean and Brazilian) settling in the 1800s, shaping Christian-associated urban culture and forming much of an African elite audience for ballroom orchestras in the 1930s–40s.. Rising coastal trade “around the turn of the twentieth century” and growing multi-ethnic communities; by the 1920s Lagos is described as containing Nigerians of every ethnicity plus Europeans/Latin Americans/foreign Africans.***ASOKO dance drumming (Christian boys’ clubs; rhythms linked to Brazilian samba). Early professional SAKARA scene recording prominency and framed through band/clubs/social engagements and mobility. Abibu Oluwa recorded late 1920s–30s; Ojo Olewale as biggest star on 1940s recordings. Yusuf Olatunji (iconic Sákárà musician), Olayiwola Ejire Early JUJU is linked to the working-class identity of YORUBA city-dwellers and to audiences of recently urbanized Yoruba and non-Yoruba transients working in Lagos and other West African ports. Nigerian Juju’s roots lie in GUITAR, BANJO, and UKULELE music emerging in the 1920s, combined with the more traditional genre ***KONKOMA (chorus, mbira-type hand-piano, drums), linked to Ghanaian-derived PALM-WINE styles popular in Lagos in the 1930s–1940s and part of an urban West African palm-wine guitar tradition. Lagos neighborhood competition: “each quarter in Lagos had its favorite juju band” (1930s). Nigeria’s record industry emerges in the early 1920s (marketing phonograms to emerging middle/upper classes); mid-1920s local recordings pressed as shellacs for sale in Nigeria. European commercial recording in/around Lagos beginning in 1928. Proto-highlife via colonial martial band → African dance-orchestra transition → Lagos-based Calabar Brass Band recording (1920s–30s) as the Lagos Mozart Orchestra. Tunde King - early juju star; first recordings with “juju” on label, Parlophone 1936. Ayinde Bakare - Yoruba migrant, recorded for HMV beginning 1937; starts as ASIKO musician; later key postwar juju figure. Irewolede Denge, Akanbi Wright (credited with introducing gangan into juju in 1948). Bobby Benson founds Jam Session Orchestra 1948; brings first electric guitar to Lagos; Urban ballroom dance orchestras in Lagos (1930s–40s) playing foxtrots/waltzes/Latin dances and arranged Yoruba songs. APALA emerges in the 1940s, integrating Yoruba elements with influences from the Muslim northern area of Nigeria, indicating cultural interaction between southern Yoruba communities and northern Nigerian Muslim regions. Haruna Ishola is cited in connection with early apala recordings, representing a leading figure. Ayinla Omowura - leading proponent of Yoruba Apala; ****Portable public-address systems introduced “during the war” and in regular Yoruba use by the late 1940s. ****Waka professional specialization “only after 1945” Nigeria’s (and Africa’s) first broadcast radio station (1950s) further popularizes Nigerian musicians. By the early 1950s, Juju is transformed by nationalism, the spread of amplification and electric guitar and the innovations of I.K. Dairo (traditional Yoruba percussion, first nigerian international star) and others like Tunde Western Nightingale, J.O. Araba, C.A. Balogun, reflecting a more self-consciously Yoruba and Nigerian popular style. 1950s remembered as the “Golden Age of Yoruba HIGHLIFE.” Lagos nightclub economy/patronage: Bobby Benson opens Caban Bamboo and employs top musicians (as a structural context for highlife). Victor Olaiya, Roy Chicago, Eddy Okonta, Rex Jim Lawson, Victor Uwaifo, Ambrose Adekoya Campbel. Apala golden age is the 1950s. Ligali Mukaiba, Kasumu Adio Guitar highlife develops in eastern Nigeria: IGBO and Efik bandleaders expand guitars and blend a new guitar-highlife style; 1960s youth adopt “guitar-style highlife.” Steven Amechi, Zeal Onyiah, Celestine Ukwu, Peacocks International; later stars include Stephen Osita Osadebe, Inyang Henshaw, Peter Effiom, Mike Ejeagha. ****Nollywood 1960s–70s I.K. Dairo and Haruna Ishola found record company STAR Records. --1968–1973, “beginning of military rule” and “end of the civil war”; oil rapidly replacing other foreign-revenue sources. Civil war (1967–1970) drives “many of the best Igbo musicians” to leave Lagos. Highlife dance bands are said to have gone out of style in Nigeria during the disruptive period of the civil war, marking a political moment that reshapes the country’s dance-band scene. Oil boom of the 1970s expanding patronage for neotraditional celebrations and increasing jùjú band number/size. AFRO-BEAT begins (late 1960s) as confluence of dance-band highlife, jazz, and soul. It is tied to Fela Kuti’s bands and Tony Allen’s drumming in the 1970s heyday of Africa 70. Fela Kuti, explicitly framed as central to modern Nigerian music, uses his Afro-beat to denounce exploitative businesses and government corruption and oppression (“Music is a weapon”); his repeated imprisonments for criticizing the Nigerian government link popular music to political dissent. Fela turns his compound into a nightclub/scene and eventually the Kalakuta Republic, declaring it independent from the Federal Republic of Nigeria; military attack on “Kalakuta Republic” (1977), subsequent political hardening and Egypt 80 shift. FUJI, rooted in Yoruba Islamic communities (succeeding Apala), emerging as genre label in the late 1960s, is described as extremely popular among Lagos lower classes, representing a new, percussion-only Nigerian genre that speaks directly to urban working-class life. Pioneered by Sikiru Ayinde Barrister, it derives from WERE and AJISARI wake-up singing tradition. Kollington Ayinla. Wasiu Ayinde Barrister. WAKA rises among Yoruba concurrent with Fuji; adopted from Muslim HAUSA ceremonies—typically women performers, vocally oriented with Yoruba talking drums/hand percussion. Batile Alake, Kubura Alaragbo, Queen Salawa Abeni are named as prominent women who popularized wákà. Among Hausa, Dan Maraya described as one of northern Nigeria’s greatest praise singers, performing primarily on Songhai/Hausa single string lute KONTIGI. In the 1970s, juju becomes further modernized and commercialized under Ebenezer Obey and King Sunny Ade, both of whom develop international audiences; this marks Nigerian juju as part of a global pop economy. Older juju songs are often praise songs for patrons or public figures; since the early 1970s, social commentary becomes more common in the texts, and religious songs abound as many juju musicians are fervent Christians. General Prince Adekunle, Lady Balogun, Moses Olaiya. Prince Nico Mbarga and Rocafil Jazz define a new style with “Sweet Mother” (1976), combining Cameroonian makossa + Igbo highlife + “a little bit of rock ’n’ roll.”; Dele Ojo (hybrid Juju-Highlife style); Lanrewaju Adepoju (Ewi poetry King); Lijadu Sisters; blind beggar-musician Kokoro B. Aderounmu. Lagos nightlife infrastructure grows: I.K. Dairo’s Kakadu, Olaiya’s venues/hotel, Sunny Ade’s Ariya Niteclub, Obey’s Miliki spot. Postwar healing highlife crop: Oriental Brothers International, Oliver deCoque, Ali Chukwuma, Nkengas. ****Sákárà: characterized by slow beat and philosophical lyrics; important in pre-independence Nigeria and early post-independence decades. ****Hubert Ogunde, ****Gospel: by the 1970s musicians emerge from church movements; by the 1980s religious music becomes popular music; ****Post-1978 transition: disputes/splintering around continuation of a leading Sákárà band after the leader’s death. 1980s economic decline/devaluation/competition reduces work for many juju groups formed in the 1970s. Osondi Owendi, Onyeka Onwenu (highlife '80s). Afro-beat continues with Femi Kuti, Seun Kuti, Made Kuti, Dede Mabiaku, Orlando Julius, Kola Ogunkoya. Hip hop / Afro-hip hop positioned as an indigenized genre among Yoruba people; Weird M.C., Mode 9, D'banj, Sound Sultan, Dagrin, 9ice, Small Doctor, Adekunle Gold, Asa. The Remedies (1997) catalyze serious domestic rap; Tony Tetuila. “Two decades after” 1968–73, observers report major change: youth knowing less of linguistic/poetic richness; traditional Hausa musicians taking wage labor and maintaining styles only occasionally. Most artists release on their own/small local labels; no centralized distribution; runaway piracy (including Asia-based manufacturing); CD/digital in the 1990s worsens the situation. Fuji described as “intensively syncretic,” incorporating Muslim recitations, Christian hymns, highlife classics, jùjú songs, Indian film themes, American pop. Adewale Ayuba, Abass Akande Obesere. Afrojuju - Shina Peters rises in 1992; described as the voice of a new generation. Reggae important since Bob Marley’s global rise in the 1970s; Majek Fashek’s early-1990s albums noted. Lagbaja emerges during the “tyrannical rule” of militar dictator Sanni Abacha (93-98) as a masked “voice of the masses.” Sunny Neji. Post-Fela “sea” of Afrobeat-influenced artists described as rising “after his death,” with many active acts named. Nigeria “returned to democratic system of government in 1999”. Apala resurgence: in 2003 Museliu Ishola updates apala while retaining its “richness and intensity,” adding occasional drum machines and rappers, with modernizing changes (tempo, slang, modern instruments) and radio/broadcast circulation. Daddy Showkey described as an “icon…innovator in Nigerian pop culture,” Kannywood (Hausa home video industry, influenced by Bollywood) described as a context for politician–musician partnerships to produce political content. Dauda Kahutu Rarara, Fati Niger, Sadiq Zazzabi, Tijjani Gandu. 2004: MTV Africa launch, enhancing Rap visibility. 2Face Idibia, Flavour N'abania, Yinka Ayefele. 2015 election is described as largely peaceful due to musicians’ appeals for peaceful elections/transfer of power.

search.title: Senegal
search.text: To the west of the Mandinka are the Tukulor, Fulɓe, Wolof, Serer and Jola (Diola)(AKONTING) collectively called Senegambians, whose languages belong to the West Atlantic subfamily. The savanna social organization for many West African societies is said to follow a stratified system similar to that of the WOLOF, with landed aristocracy, hereditary military class, craft guilds, free peasants, hereditary house servants and slaves.Portuguese presence in Senegal in the 15th century. - First French settlements established in 1659. Early 19th century: Mande legacy “reinforced” by an influx of griots from Mali after the break-up of the Bamana empires. Alongside jaliyaa, the text implies a contrasting “folk” sphere of dance drumming and singing: all-male drum troupes perform for varied village events, mostly involving women, who are also the main subject of the songs. Late 19th century: Senegal becomes the administrative base of France’s West African empire. 1960: Léopold Sédar Senghor (first president; poet) as prime negritude exponent; his commitment to culture leads to promotion of griot music via troupes/ensembles. Star Band de Dakar formed by Ibrahim Kassé to play at Senegal’s independence celebrations. Few Senegalese had access to recorded music; dance bands attached to nightclubs serving a small bourgeois elite seeking “sophisticated” Western sounds; outkast Yakhya Fall later forms Star Number One together with Papa Serigne Seck; traditional music stigmatized as “primitive” and “shameful” (linked to caste associations). Cuban and Latin covers dominate; gradual “Africanization” (Cuban songs adapted into Wolof; traditional Wolof/Mandinka songs and rhythms introduced). Djimo Kouyate was an early member of Ensemble Instrumental Traditionnel du Senegal and later founder of Ensemble National des Ballets du Senegal. Late 60s - Dakar nightclub scene strongly oriented to Cuban/Latin music; Cuban songs adapted into Wolof; traditional songs/rhythms introduced into dance-band settings. 1970: Dakar described as still “in many ways a French city”; Baobab Club created by businessmen/politicians in the Plateau (European quarter) becomes a major cultural node; veteran Star Band saxman Baro Ndiaye recruited guitarist Barthelemy Attisso, singer Rudy Gomis and percussionist Balla Sidibe to form Orchestra Baobab, together with Wolof griot Laye Mboup, bringing neo-Islamic sounds, and Nigerian saxophonist Peter Udo, introducing highlife touch. Late 1970s: social/cultural balance shifts toward the quartiers populaires; a “pop revolution” emerges around a young Youssou N’Dour and a raw new music called MBALAX. He founds proud Wolof-language pop stardom Etoile de Dakar in 1977, together with El Hadji Faye; addresses youth of a rapidly urbanizing, demographically exploding country. Super Diamono de Dakar: reggae-inspired militancy + jazz cool + Senegalese Sufi mysticism; Abdoulaye Prosper Niang founds Xalam, new thing jazz tastes band, and later works with griot Souleymane Faye; Early 1980s: N’Dour begins tackling social themes (economic migration, African identity, apartheid), explicitly “expanding the role of the griot” toward social critic/political commentator. Postwar-to-present thread noted: popular Islam/Sufi brotherhoods’ influence pervades even pop music (noted as a major influence on migrants/urban culture). Additional “superstar” names join Senegal’s pantheon, like Baaba Maal, Thione Seck, Ismaël Lô, Mansour Seck, Touré Kunda, First international release by a Senegalese woman recorded in 1989 by griotte Kiné Lam, followed by traditional divas named Daro Mbaye, Madiodio, Khar Mbaye Madiaga. Producers/entrepreneurs include Laminé Faye, Cheikh Tidiane Tall, Papis Konaté; Mid-1990s: Generation Boul Fale signaled by Alioune Mbaye Nder’s Thiossane nightclub performances; described as a youth attitude toward authority/politics. Omar Pène leads Super Diamono as singer. Baaba Maal’s working process on “Firin’ in Fouta” is anchored in the country’s geography: he returns to his ancestral village Podor in the north, records local indigenous performance there, then moves to Dakar to create studio rhythm tracks, and finally travels to England to complete the project. Malick Pathé Sow, Morikeba Kouyate. Coumba Gawlo framed as griotte with modern image, commenting on social issues. Fatou Laobé: neo-traditional figure specializing in tassou; tassou described as originally performed after marriages by women of the Laobe woodworking caste (with dancing). Hip-hop figures and roles: Positive Black Soul (Didier Awadi; Duggy-Tee), Daara J, Pee Froiss (leader Xuman).

search.title: Sierra Leone
search.text: Most speakers of West Atlantic languages—Temne, Sherbro, Limba, Gola, Kissi—live in Sierra Leone. Temne history is sketched as migration from the mountainous region of Jallonkadu (later part of Futa Djallon) to the coast north of the Sherbro.There is considerable variety of music even within each group, and it would be futile to try and cut up Sierra Leone music into tribal sections. Freetown is shaped by Caribbean freed slave immigrants, who give the capital its name and an enduring KRIO culture, creating a cosmopolitan, coastal urban setting for later musical development. KRU sailors from Liberia work on foreign ships, including early Portuguese vessels that bring guitars, which they adopt and spread along the West African coast. Early moral panic around GUMBAY (african musical style repatriated from jamaican MAROON) is documented in 1858, when the African and Sierra Leone Weekly Advertiser journal denounces 'Gumbay dancing' as a cause of vices. Gumbay is played by Ebenezer Calendar, whose "African Elegant - Sierra Leone's Kru / Krio Calypso Connection" recordings document a coastal Kru and Freetown Krio musical life, tiying to CALYPSO song forms and leanding to MARINGA, local name for PALM-WINE music. Sierra Leone gains independence from Britain in 1961. From then onward, it suffers gross mismanagement, coups d’état, neo-colonial pressures and a venal, entrenched elite, undermining what should be a prosperous, resource-rich country. Ebenezer Calendar is a mainstay of the Sierra Leone Broadcasting Service, whose recordings made for radio in the late 1950s/early 1960s capture both his independence-era songs and traditional material from communities all over the country. S.E. Rogie develops an "effortlessly laidback" palmwine guitar style. HIGHLIFE, after its decline in popularity since the mid-1960s, contributed to the evolution of several regional forms that continue to be popular, like the stronger rock and disco orientation MILO-JAZZ, popularized by Dr. Oloh and his Milo-Jazz Band. The 1970s are explicitly named as Sierra Leone’s musical heyday, when bands that grew up in the years after independence develop their own styles and sing about "sweet Salone" (krio for Sierra Leone), "swinging Freetown" and romantic/sexual themes. Their often explicit lyrics bring some bands into conflict with the post-independence authorities. Groups such as Afro National, Muyei Power, Sabanoh 75 and Super Combo Kings forge a style dubbed SOCA-BEAT. Geraldo Pino crafts a heavy funky big-band sound, influencing development of AFRO-BEAT and Afro-Pop. Bunny Mack and Abou Whyte. Even as creativity peaks, the national recording industry "dies" in the 1970s. In the 1980s and 1990s, the few notable success stories are largely those of exiled musicians recording and performing abroad. Eleven years of civil war (1991–2002) further devastate the nation; war and economic hardship contribute to the disappearance of certain local styles and limit the possibilities for cultural life. U.S.A. based Daddy Ramanu uses a combination of "traditional" and calypso/highlife influences to create dancefloor-oriented beats. King Masco’s 1990s output consists of palmwine-based, ribald songs aimed at Sierra Leonean audiences at home and abroad. Abdul Tee-Jay, veteran London-based multi-instrumentalist. German based Ansumana Bangura howcases his "fankadama" approach, combining highlife, palmwine, traditional society music and milo-jazz into uptempo, percussive tracks. Great Steady Bongo maintains a presence within Sierra Leone. Ngoh Gbetuwai, Mende musician. Seydu, Freetown-born multi-instrumentalist influenced by his Fulani-Mandinka mother’s chanting. In the late 1990s, returning exile Jimmy B establishes the Paradise studio in Freetown, which becomes a launch pad for a new generation of artists like Sisters With Attitude and Janka Nabay. Postwar youth frustration with corrupt leaders is encapsulated in Daddy Saj’s and Wan Pot Sojas' hits. A large gospel industry, with artists like Vicky Fornah and Johnny Wisdom, prospers among listeners primarily interested in religious messages rather than musical innovation.

search.title: Togo
search.text: Togo straddles both savanna (north) and forest/coastal (south) zones of West Africa, so its musical life reflects both savanna traditions (Voltaic and Central Sudanic influences, Islamic-linked professional specialists) and forest/coastal traditions (Aja/Ewe microstates, elaborate court and vodun ceremonies, masquerades, and dense dance-club networks. Among the EWE of Togo, regional differences in scale and harmony persist: northern Ewe music favors a seven-tone diatonic system with polyphony in thirds (borrowed from neighboring AKAN), while southern ANLO-EWE use a five-tone scale with harmony in parallel fourths and a generally lower vocal tessitura. Northern GUMBAY music and traditional southern AGBADJA are identified as long-standing traditions that feed into new styles like GOUMBEJA; their existence is presented as pre-dating contemporary RAP / REGGAE experiments. - 1967–1973: President Gnassingbé Eyadéma is described as a “tyrant” whose 38 years of undivided rule, where music has “not had a high profile” in Togo, are only ending with his recent death (2005). Togo is represented on high-profile West African and international stages by Bella Bellow, whose career marks an early modern Togolese presence in the wider region; she becomes a model for emotive, romance-focused popular song, inspiring a succession of Togolese female singers: Yta Jourias, Mabah, Afia Mala. - Mid-1980s: In the Togolese capital Lomé, the Africa New Sound studio operates as one of Africa’s most sophisticated 24-track recording facilities, attracting artists such as Abeti Masikini and Dr. Nico (both from Congo). - early 1990s–c. 2000: “Social unrest and military violence” shake Togo, particularly affecting youth; people fear holding parties at home because of militia punitive expeditions. The situation “hinders the careers” of talented musicians on the national scene, prompting many to move to Europe, or across the border to Benin or Cameroon. Jimi Hope creates his own “heady mix of rock and tropical rhythms,” coupled with lyrics that openly denounce abuses of power. Fifi Rafiatou gains some international success singing in IFE and Ewe dialects. - 2001–2004: - King Mensah AFRO-BEAT to REGGAE spectrum – his music is “driven by powerful percussion deeply rooted in African traditions”. Field recordings of Kabiyé Orchestras and Lithophones (Ewe traditional music) in northern Togo document agricultural-year music and instruments, indicating parallel attention to heritage while youth scenes grow. 2003: Launch of the Togo Hip-Hop Awards ceremony. December 2004: Second staging of the Africarap Festival, backing the awards and signalling institutional support for HIP-HOP (Dzoku-Kay, Djantakan, Small Poppy, Eric M.C., Wedy, RX Patou).

search.title: West Africa
search.text: West Africa is portrayed as the part of Africa where polyrhythmic, multilayered music is especially evident, shaped by a heritage of cultural interchange with North African and Arab traditions, particularly in savannas and deserts. Across West Africa, the figure of the professional or semiprofessional musician tends to occupy a distinct and often hereditary social niche, mediating between rulers, ancestors, spirits and communities through historical song, praise and ritual performance, who were vital parts of state occasions. Traditional structures, religious practices, hereditary court-based musician roles and dense networks of dance clubs remain central features of social and ceremonial life, indicating only moderate adjustment and continuity of precolonial practices into the contemporary era. In the savanna region, there is much uniformity in musical culture, particularly in social organization, musician roles and status, types of instruments and styles of performance, although differences remain between regional clusters (Western Sudanic, Central Sudanic, Voltaic). Because of ongoing contacts, Central Sudanic music is relatively uniform: North-African influence is most evident in ceremonial music and instrument types; Hausa music dominates the cluster, influencing central and southwest Nigeria, the Guinea coast and Voltaic peoples. Courtly ensemble performance for state occasions is treated as part of a general pattern shared by ancient West African empires, whose wealth from long-distance trade allowed to maintain large ensembles of royal musicians. Their performances acted as sonic symbols that paralleled visual symbols of power such as cloth and gold-covered swords, stools and staves. Forest-belt music is characterized by complex rhythm, extensive use of percussive instruments, and elaborated court and masquerade traditions. Musicians provide soundtracks for life-cycle events, agricultural work, festivals, religious rites and political. The Eastern Forest cluster, used as a model for West African forest music, is characterized by smaller-scale nation-states or confederacies, age-grade systems and secret societies, with external influences from savanna dwellers and Europeans. Across West Africa, praise-singing griots or jeli are highlighted as a key professional musician type; they often come from families of musicians who train their children to carry on the occupation, embodying a hereditary model of musical specialization within the region. In each Western Sudanic ethnic group, professional or full-time musicians bear specific titles; for example, dyeli among the Manding of Mali, jali among Maninka of Guinea and Mandinka of The Gambia, gewel among Wolof, and gawlo among Fulɓe. The Central Sudanic cluster (Songhai, Djerma, Dendi, Hausa, Fulani, Kanuri, Jukun, Tiv) mostly live in Nigeria, Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso; groups in the Central Sudanic cluster did not experience a major dismantling of their traditional social structure as a result of colonial policies. Consequently, patronage and social stratification remain more intact than in the Western Sudanic cluster. In Central Sudanic cultures (HAUSA, FULANI, DAGBAMBA), musicians are largely full-time specialists and urbanites belonging to a distinct social class. Ceremonial musicians linked to traditional power hold high status, while others enjoy lower but still recognized status. Musical styles are strongly text-driven: melody and rhythm track the tones and quantities of tonal languages, and instruments often imitate speech; solo or small-ensemble singing with dense melismatic ornamentation is common. Historically, West Africa includes centralized kingdoms (such as Mali), “stateless societies” with less hierarchical chief-based structures and nomadic peoples that coexist alongside modern national governments. - West Africa’s savanna zone, is the setting for major empires (Ghana to about 1200, Mali 1200s–1400s), influencing trade and population movements. - After about 1600, the history of the Sudanic empires is described as one of fracture and gradual decline, affected by internal rebellions. - 1591 - Songhai invaded by Moroccan expeditionary force; 1700s - the Atlantic slave trade; - 1800s - Islamic jihads; European colonial administration expansion and Christian missionaries take firm control of the Gold Coast after the abolition of the slave trade, using music (regimental bands, classical concerts, theatre, Christian hymns and anthems) to create “punctual, disciplined and civilized” workers and to counter “pagan” drumming and dancing; - In the Sudanic desert countries, Congolese music and other imported forms previously tended to dominate dance repertoires before the late 1970s. Secular much religions, secret societies and rites Islam reaches Africa by the 7th century; by the 18th–19th centuries, Muslim trading networks and Sufi brotherhoods wield significant political influence in West Africa, linking regions via lineage, trade and religious networks.

search.title: Africa
search.text: Africa is a huge continent. - From the 16th century, the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade carries enslaved Africans and their traditional musics to the Americas; - After slavery abolition in the 19th century, repatriated freed slaves and their descendants’ musics (jazz, blues, calypso, reggae) influence neo-traditional and contemporary African art forms. - Early 1980s shift to musicassettes: the spread of domestic cassette players revolutionizes the creation, performance and distribution of music; piracy emerges via widespread “duplicator” businesses and international companies reduce investment; major studios begin coasting on existing equipment.
